stem: A patient was planned for total knee replacement and the surgeon was about to make the incision on the wrong leg, a nurse knew but kept quite, one of the staff checked the patient's file before the incision and discovered it's the wrong leg, how to prevent such case?
OptA: Nurse shouldn't say anything and assume that surgeon knows better
OptB: Review the patient's chart
OptC: Proper marking prior to the surgery
why_right: The lead in asks "how to prevent such case", meaning a system level safeguard against wrong site surgery. Under the Universal Protocol and the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, the key preventive step is proper site marking before surgery: the operating surgeon marks the site with an indelible marker before the patient enters the theatre, ideally with the awake patient confirming it, followed by the time out before incision.
why_wrong_block:
A. Staying silent is the very failure that allowed this near miss; every team member is expected to speak up, and anyone may stop the procedure if the site is in doubt.
B. Reviewing the chart is part of preprocedure verification and is what caught the error here, but on its own it is a late, unreliable check; the visible site mark plus time out is the standard preventive measure.
key_concept:
Universal Protocol to prevent wrong patient, wrong procedure, wrong site surgery.
  • Step 1: preprocedure verification (identity, procedure, consent, records, imaging).
  • Step 2: site marking by the operating surgeon, before entering the OR, patient awake if possible, mark visible after draping.
  • Step 3: time out immediately before incision with the whole team.
  • Any team member who notices a discrepancy must speak up (stop the line).
exam_pearl: A near miss caught by a chart check still points to marking before surgery as the prevention, not to the chart review.
compiler_note: Compiler note: AboSarah: (Patient safety & surgical error prevention). Near-miss wrong-site surgery, a serious and preventable error. Per WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, Joint Commission and standard protocols, the most effective preventive step is proper site marking before surgery: site marked clearly, usually by the operating surgeon, before the patient enters the OR, with the patient awake when possible, using an indelible marker. Part of the Universal Protocol to prevent wrong patient, wrong procedure, wrong site surgery.

stem: An orthopedic surgeon completed a fellowship in spinal surgery and finished the program on time. He is now requesting clinical privileges to perform Complex spinal surgeries in the hospital. What should you ( Do as Certificant Provider do ) Smt like that?
OptA: Grant privileges based on his years of experience
OptB: Approve privileges based on completion of the Cirtificat Solely
OptC: Do not grant privileges until he completes at least 2 years of Site clinical practice
OptD: assess competency of his performance Before certification
highlight_terms_source: completed a fellowship in spinal surgery
why_right: Clinical privileges are granted on demonstrated, current competence for the specific procedures requested, not on titles or time served. For a surgeon newly requesting "complex spinal surgeries", the hospital should verify training and assess his actual performance and competency (for example case logs, evaluations from the program, and a period of proctored or focused evaluation) before granting privileges.
why_wrong_block:
A. Years of general orthopaedic experience do not prove competence in the specific new procedure; privileges are procedure specific.
B. A certificate shows completion of training, not verified competence; credentialing requires assessment of performance, not the certificate alone.
C. An arbitrary waiting period of practice is not a competency criterion; once competence is verified he can be privileged without a fixed delay.
key_concept:
Credentialing and privileging are competency based and procedure specific.
  • Credentialing: verify licence, training and certificates from primary sources.
  • Privileging: decide which procedures he may perform, based on evidence of competence.
  • New privileges are usually followed by a focused period of performance evaluation, then ongoing review.
exam_pearl: Certificate or years alone never earn privileges; documented competence does.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Alternate recall (Q:): Fellow neurosurgeon came to fellowship and finished on time now he asks to preform spinal surgeries in that hospital what will u tell him? A- He can because he was good preforming; B- He can because he is educated; C- He cannot until at least 2 y post clinical; D- He can if u reassure he had good performance (highlighted, consistent with D).

stem: An elderly patient with a known history of ischemic heart disease underwent CABG. A few days after surgery, he developed a surgical site infection that progressed to septicemia. Despite appropriate management, the patient's condition worsened to multiorgan failure, and he ultimately died. Which of the following should be recorded as the primary cause of death in his death certificate?
OptB: Ischemic heart disease
OptC: Congestive heart failure
OptD: CABG
highlight_terms_source: surgical site infection that progressed to septicemia
primary cause of death in his death certificate
why_right: The lead in asks for the cause to record, and this recall's key is Septicemia: after CABG the patient developed a "surgical site infection that progressed to septicemia", and that septic process is what led directly to the fatal "multiorgan failure". Multiorgan failure itself is only a mode of dying and is not accepted as a cause, so the recall records the disease process that drove it.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ischemic heart disease is the background condition for which CABG was done; in this recall's reading the death followed the infective complication, so IHD is listed lower in the chain rather than as the keyed cause.
C. Congestive heart failure is not described anywhere in the chain; it is also a vague terminal state that should not be entered as a cause without a stated underlying disease.
D. A procedure is not a disease; CABG is recorded as part of the sequence (the operation complicated by infection), not as the cause of death.
key_concept:
Death certificate Part I runs from the immediate cause (top line) down to the underlying cause (lowest line).
  • Immediate cause: the final disease or complication directly causing death (here septicemia, leading to multiorgan failure).
  • Underlying cause (WHO): the disease or injury that initiated the train of events; this is the one used for statistics.
  • Chain here: IHD, then CABG, then surgical site infection, then septicemia, then multiorgan failure, then death.
  • Modes of dying (cardiac arrest, multiorgan failure) are not causes.
  • Procedures and their complications are written in the sequence, not as the underlying cause.
exam_pearl: If the question says "underlying" cause, go to the bottom of the chain; if it says "immediate" or "direct", go to the top.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: After long research the compiler concluded the final cause is what is written on the death certificate. My answer is A- Septicemia. Per UpToDate guidance, list the underlying condition that started the chain of events leading directly and inevitably to death (underlying cause on the lowest line of Part I). Another answer: WHO definition: the disease or injury which initiated the train of morbid events leading directly to death. Chain: IHD, CABG, Septicemia, Multiorgan failure, Death.
Other marked answers: Highlighted: B. Ischemic heart disease

stem: Pregnant lady was advised to do Caesarean section due to Cephalo-pelvic Disproportion (CPD); the mother refused to do the surgery even when they explained the indication.
OptB: Start anaesthesia & do the surgery
OptC: Call her husband, explain & take his consent
highlight_terms_source: the mother refused to do the surgery
why_right: A competent adult woman who has had the indication explained ("even when they explained the indication") has the right to refuse surgery, even a cesarean for cephalopelvic disproportion. Maternal autonomy is respected over fetal interest, so the team respects her decision, documents the informed refusal, keeps offering the best care she will accept, and gives her the chance to change her mind.
why_wrong_block:
B. Operating on a competent patient who refuses is a violation of autonomy and amounts to assault; emergency treatment without consent applies only when the patient lacks capacity.
C. A husband cannot consent on behalf of a competent adult wife or override her refusal; his consent would only matter if she lacked capacity and he were the legal surrogate.
key_concept:
Competent adult + informed refusal = respect it, even if life or fetus is at risk.
  • Confirm capacity and that the risks were understood.
  • Document the informed refusal.
  • Continue care within her consent and revisit the discussion.
  • Spouse, relatives or administration cannot override a competent patient.
  • Act without consent only when the patient lacks capacity in an emergency.
exam_pearl: Pregnancy does not remove autonomy: no option to force surgery or take the husband's consent is correct for a competent woman.

stem: Couple are infertile and the husband has frozen sperms in the clinic, and then the husband died; then the wife goes to the clinic wanting to use these sperms.
OptA: Must be three consultations and then can use it
OptB: Should the family of husband agree
OptC: She can't use sperms of a dead person
OptD: She can use it if there was consent from her husband
why_right: The husband has died, and in the Saudi/Islamic framework that SMLE follows, the marriage contract ends with death. Assisted reproduction is permitted only between a husband and wife during a valid marriage, so his frozen sperm cannot be used by the widow and should be discarded per regulations.
why_wrong_block:
A. Repeated consultations do not change the legal and religious status: no number of counselling sessions makes posthumous use permissible.
B. The husband's family has no authority over his gametes or over the widow's reproduction; their agreement cannot legitimise use after the marriage has ended.
D. Prior written consent of the husband is what permits posthumous use in some Western jurisdictions, but under Saudi regulations even his consent cannot override the end of the marriage at death.
key_concept:
Saudi ART rule: gametes and embryos may be used only between a living husband and wife within a valid marriage.
  • Husband dies: frozen sperm/embryos cannot be used; they are discarded.
  • Divorce ends permission too.
  • No third party: donor sperm, donor eggs and surrogacy are not permitted.
exam_pearl: Option D (husband's consent) is the trap: posthumous use with prior consent is allowed in some Western countries, but for SMLE death ends the marriage and no consent revives permission.

stem: A military service member says he has low back pain and requests two weeks of sick leave. On examination, muscle power is normal, there are no neurological deficits, and the patient is sitting comfortably.
OptA: Do not give sick leave, advise to be committed to work
OptB: Give one week of sick leave
OptC: Give two weeks of sick leave
OptD: Do not give sick leave and advise muscle relaxation exercises
highlight_terms_source: requests two weeks of sick leave
muscle power is normal, there are no neurological deficits
why_right: The examination is reassuring: normal power, no neurological deficit, sitting comfortably. This is simple mechanical low back pain that does not justify two weeks off, so sick leave is not medically indicated. The doctor still has a duty to treat the complaint, so he gives advice such as muscle relaxation exercises and staying active.
why_wrong_block:
A. Refusing leave is correct, but only lecturing him to be committed to work dismisses his complaint and gives no treatment; a doctor manages the symptom, not the patient's motivation.
B. A week of leave is not justified by a normal examination, and bed rest or inactivity slows recovery in simple back pain.
C. Granting the full two weeks just because he requests it means certifying unfitness without clinical grounds, which is dishonest certification.
key_concept:
Sick leave is a medical certificate: issue it only when objective findings justify it.
  • Normal exam, no red flags: no leave, reassurance, stay active, exercises and simple analgesia.
  • Red flags (deficit, saddle anaesthesia, sphincter change, fever, weight loss, trauma): investigate.
  • Never certify more than the clinical picture supports.
exam_pearl: Choose the option that both refuses unjustified leave and still treats the patient; plain refusal alone is the trap.

stem: A group of researchers are doing a study by gathering people with Alzheimer's disease and giving them fish oil. What is the primary approach that is used by the IRB to assess the ethical acceptability of the research study?
OptB: Deontology
OptC: Ethical skepticism
OptD: Comparativeism
why_right: This recall's key is Deontology because research ethics committees judge a study by duties and rules owed to each participant: informed consent (here from people with Alzheimer's disease, who may lack capacity), respect for persons and protection of the vulnerable. A study is unacceptable if it violates these duties even when the expected societal benefit is large, which is duty-based rather than outcome-based reasoning.
why_wrong_block:
A. Utilitarianism judges an act only by the greatest good for the greatest number; an IRB does weigh risks against benefits, but it will not approve harming or using individuals just because overall benefit is high.
C. Ethical skepticism doubts that objective moral knowledge exists; it is a philosophical position, not a framework for approving research.
D. Comparativeism is not a recognised framework used for research ethics review.
key_concept:
Ethical theories in one line each:
  • Deontology: duty and rules; the act is right or wrong in itself (consent, honesty).
  • Utilitarianism / consequentialism: best overall outcome.
  • Virtue ethics: what would a good doctor do.
  • Principlism: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice.
exam_pearl: Vulnerable participants plus 'IRB' points to duty-based protection of individuals, not maximising benefit.

stem: A surgeon conducted a research study on a new surgical procedure that was supposed to have fewer complications. During one of the operations, a patient developed bleeding. The surgeon decided to remove this case from the research report to make the results look better. Which ethical principle did the surgeon violate?
OptB: Research Justice
OptC: Integrity
OptD: Non-maleficence
highlight_terms_source: remove this case from the research report
why_right: The surgeon removed a complication case from the report to make the results look better. Deliberately altering or omitting data is falsification, which breaches research integrity (honesty and accuracy in conducting and reporting research). The harm is to the truthfulness of the evidence, not to the patient on the table.
why_wrong_block:
A. Beneficence is the duty to act in the patient's best interest; nothing here shows he failed to treat or help the bleeding patient.
B. Research justice concerns fair selection of participants and fair distribution of research burdens and benefits, not honest reporting of results.
D. Non-maleficence concerns causing harm to the patient; the bleeding was a complication, and the wrongdoing is in hiding it from the data.
key_concept:
Research misconduct (FFP) violates integrity:
  • Fabrication: making up data or results.
  • Falsification: manipulating or omitting data so results are misrepresented.
  • Plagiarism: using others' work or words without credit.
exam_pearl: If 'Integrity' or 'Honesty' is missing in a recall, pick the option about truthful reporting, not the patient care principles.
compiler_note: Compiler note: The surgeon intentionally removed a complication (bleeding case) from the results to make the procedure appear safer; this is data falsification / selective reporting, violating research integrity and honesty. Note: in a newer recall 'Integrity' was not present in the options (A. Beneficence, B. Research Justice, C. ?, D. Non-maleficence).

stem: A physician was working on a research paper. Before publishing the paper, he made some changes to some of the data and omitted other parts of his results. What is this action referred to?
OptB: Fabrication
OptC: Plagiarism
highlight_terms_source: made some changes to some of the data
omitted other parts of his results
why_right: He worked with real data but changed some of it and omitted other results. Manipulating or selectively leaving out genuine data so the record no longer reflects the research is the definition of falsification.
why_wrong_block:
B. Fabrication means inventing data or results that were never collected; here the data existed and were altered or dropped.
C. Plagiarism is presenting another person's ideas, words or results as your own without credit; nothing was taken from others here.
key_concept:
Fabricate = make up; Falsify = change or omit real data; Plagiarise = steal credit.
  • Omitting inconvenient results counts as falsification.
  • All three are research misconduct.
exam_pearl: The key word is 'changed or omitted' (falsification) versus 'invented' (fabrication).

stem: A 16 y/o found out that she is pregnant and decided to terminate pregnancy due to financial problems and she is afraid her educational plan will be affected, she ask about information for abortion which was against doctor idea
OptA: Respect her decision and provide unbiased information
OptB: Do not provide information because of the doctor personnel opinion
OptC: The doctor should not provide anything as this is illegal and may cause illegal issues
OptD: Report her to the authorities because it is illegal
why_right: The doctor's own view (against the doctor's idea) must not block the patient's access to accurate information. The ethical duty is to respect her autonomy, give non-judgemental, unbiased counselling on all options including what is legally permitted, and support her decision making, as the patient has a right to information about her own care.
why_wrong_block:
B. Personal beliefs may allow a doctor to decline to perform a procedure, but never to withhold information; at minimum he must inform and refer.
C. Giving information is not illegal; refusing all help abandons the patient and pushes her toward unsafe options.
D. Asking about abortion is not a crime to report; reporting her breaches confidentiality and destroys trust.
key_concept:
Conscientious objection limits what you DO, not what you TELL.
  • Give full, unbiased information on options and the legal position.
  • Keep confidentiality.
  • If you will not participate, refer to a colleague.
exam_pearl: Options that withhold information or report the patient are always wrong in counselling questions.

stem: patient with severe preeclampsia, doctor recommended to terminate pregnancy, both parent refused, how to manage?
OptB: respect their wishes to continue pregnancy
OptC: to be reviewed by ethical committee then decide
OptD: ignore their wishes
why_right: The doctor has recommended termination and explained the situation, and the couple refused. A competent, informed patient may refuse treatment even when it is risky, so her wishes are respected; the doctor documents the informed refusal, keeps monitoring and treating within her consent, and leaves the door open for her to change her mind.
why_wrong_block:
A. Referring to another doctor does not address the informed refusal and only delays care in a dangerous condition.
C. An ethics committee cannot override the decision of a competent patient; it is used for genuine dilemmas such as lack of capacity, not for clear informed refusal.
D. Ignoring their wishes and terminating anyway is treatment without consent, violating autonomy and amounting to assault.
key_concept:
Competent informed refusal is respected, even if life threatening.
  • Explain risks clearly, confirm capacity.
  • Document the refusal.
  • Continue the best care she accepts and keep re-offering.
  • Husband or relatives cannot consent or refuse for a competent adult.
exam_pearl: Override is allowed only when the patient lacks capacity or in an emergency with no decision maker; a competent refusal stands.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Shown as 'Q:' within the 428 block; a different question.

stem: A Junior doctor in a private hospital notices senior doctor manipulating documentation and doing unnecessary procedures for money. Junior reports him, issue subsides. Now senior gives junior an alarming letter. What to do?
OptB: Go to senior directly
OptC: Document the misconduct to preserve your legal rights
why_right: The junior acted properly by reporting the misconduct, and is now being intimidated by a warning letter from the senior. The safe and professional step is to keep a clear, factual written record of the misconduct and of the retaliation, which protects his legal position and supports any escalation through official channels.
why_wrong_block:
A. Staying silent lets the retaliation and the original misconduct continue and leaves the junior unprotected.
B. Confronting the senior directly, after a report has already been made, risks escalating the conflict and gives no formal protection; concerns go through official channels.
key_concept:
Whistleblowing ladder: document facts, report through the proper institutional channel, escalate to the regulator if unresolved.
  • Keep dated, factual records.
  • Retaliation is itself reportable.
exam_pearl: When threatened after reporting, documentation first, never silence or personal confrontation.

stem: new e-research study on the gastritis patient and the use of 2 different NSAIDs. The participation in the study will be through an online interview. What is the ethical errors in there research?
OptB: Information gathering is not accurate
OptC: Informed consent cannot be monitored
OptD: Participant cannot get out of the interview
why_right: Participation is through an online interview about personal health data (gastritis and drug effects). Electronic collection and transmission of identifiable health information carries the main ethical risk of loss of confidentiality, so privacy is the key concern this recall targets.
why_wrong_block:
B. Accuracy of information is a methodological or validity issue, not an ethical error in the research design.
C. Consent can be obtained and documented electronically; difficulty monitoring it is a lesser concern than exposure of participants' data.
D. Participants can stop an online interview at any time; the right to withdraw is not lost because the study is online.
key_concept:
E-research ethics: main risk is privacy and data security.
  • Protect identifiable data (encryption, anonymisation, secure storage).
  • Consent and the right to withdraw still apply online.
exam_pearl: Online or electronic data collection in an ethics question points to privacy and confidentiality.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q (other version): Ethics case, e-research for 2 drugs and their effects on group of patients, why is the e-research not good for ethics? Options: Patient can't withdraw once participate / no privacy (highlighted) / Consent can not be monitored.

stem: A Doctor Has Been Practicing Internal Medicine For 10 Years, But He Knows That He Is Weak Regarding Immunology. What Should He Do To Improve?
OptB: Read More Articles Regarding Immunology In His Free Time
OptC: Attend Conferences And Workshops
why_right: He has identified a specific knowledge gap (immunology) and wants the latest therapies. Structured continuing medical education, such as accredited conferences and workshops, is the recognised way to stay current with new evidence and practice.
why_wrong_block:
A. Asking colleagues is useful for a single case but is informal and may not reflect the latest evidence.
B. Reading articles helps, but unstructured reading in free time is less reliable for a deliberate update on new therapies than formal CME.
key_concept: Lifelong learning: recognise the gap, then use structured CME (conferences, workshops, accredited courses) to close it.
exam_pearl: For 'stay updated on latest therapies', choose the formal CME option over informal ones.

stem: Elderly patient k/c of osteoporosis with minimal benefit of NSAIDS and physical therapy. Orthopedic consultant suggested for him surgical intervention which involves new knee implant that was just approved. This procedure is expensive in compare to the other alternatives. The surgeon will receive a bouns for every patient undergoes this procedure in the hospital. And he didn't explain for him other interventions rather than surgery (this part is from the person who wrote the recall previously, it was not mentioned in the my exam as I remember)
OptA: He didn't explain the risk of surgery
OptB: the patient should have been referred to a second opinion
OptC: surgeon financial interest might affects the choice of knee implant (or something similar to this)
OptD: it is just a mild disease and surgery is not needed
why_right: The core ethical problem is a conflict of interest: the surgeon "will receive a bonus for every patient" who has this new, expensive implant. A financial incentive tied to one specific procedure can bias the recommendation away from the patient's best interest, so it must be disclosed and should not drive the choice. The other options are either not supported by the stem or are not the key ethical breach.
why_wrong_block:
A. The stem says nothing about risks being withheld; failure to explain risks would be an informed consent issue, which would be the answer only if the scenario stated it.
B. A second opinion is the patient's right when he asks for one, but he did not request it here, and referral does not address the real problem (the surgeon's bonus).
D. The disease failed NSAIDs and physical therapy, so surgery is not obviously unnecessary; judging severity is a clinical point, not the ethical issue tested.
key_concept:
Conflict of interest = a personal (often financial) gain that can bias clinical judgement.
  • Bonus per procedure, industry payments, owning the device company = conflict of interest
  • Manage it: disclose to the patient, put patient interest first, offer alternatives
  • Informed consent must include risks, benefits AND alternatives
  • Second opinion: offered when the patient requests it or doubts the plan
exam_pearl: When a stem mentions a bonus, commission or payment linked to a test or procedure, the answer is the conflict of interest.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Note on option B: the patient did not request this in the scenario.

stem: A multiparous patient who had delivered 6 babies previously all of which through CS now wants to deliver her 7th baby by CS. The doctors recommended tube ligation to prevent serious complications with future pregnancies. What is the best action
OptA: Take consent from her or her representative
OptB: Take consent from both husband
OptC: Take consent from her and tell her to inform her husband
OptD: Consult ethics committee
why_right: This recall's key is to take consent from her and advise her to inform her husband. She is a competent adult, and tubal ligation here is medically recommended (6 previous CS, risk of "serious complications with future pregnancies"), so her own informed consent is what makes the procedure valid. Encouraging her to tell her husband respects the shared nature of family decisions without making his signature a condition.
why_wrong_block:
A. A representative only consents when the patient lacks capacity; she is competent, so consent must come from her directly.
B. Making the husband's consent mandatory overrides a competent woman's autonomy over a medically indicated procedure; joint spousal agreement is the classic answer for elective contraception disputes, not this case.
D. An ethics committee is for genuine unresolved dilemmas (capacity doubt, conflicting duties); here there is a competent patient and a clear medical indication.
key_concept:
Competent adult = she signs her own consent.
  • Representative/guardian consent only if she lacks capacity
  • Husband cannot sign in place of a competent wife
  • Elective contraception disagreements: answer keys often favour mutual spousal agreement
  • Medically indicated sterilization: patient consents; encourage involving the husband
exam_pearl: "Competent adult + medically indicated" points to her own consent; elective family planning disputes are where mutual consent appears.

stem: Patient With Lung cancer and pneumonia That is TREATED COMPLETELY, the patient passed away and the doctor was going to write in the report that cancer is the cause of death but the patient family refused and insisted it was pneumonia, best action?
OptA: Write pneumonia as the cause of death
OptB: Write lung cancer as the cause of death
OptC: Write that pneumonia was a contributing factor to death
why_right: The pneumonia was "TREATED COMPLETELY", so it was no longer active and did not cause the death; the lung cancer did. A death certificate is a legal document and must state the true medical cause, so the doctor writes lung cancer even though the family objects. Family wishes cannot change factual documentation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Writing pneumonia would be falsifying the certificate to please the family; it would only be right if active pneumonia had actually caused the death.
C. A resolved pneumonia did not contribute to the death, so listing it as contributing is still inaccurate; it is the answer only when pneumonia was active at death (see the untreated version of this recall).
key_concept:
Death certificate = honest, legal record of the medical cause of death.
  • Family requests never change the documented cause
  • Treated, resolved condition: not part of the cause of death
  • Active condition at death in a cancer patient: recorded as well, alongside the cancer
  • Explain gently to the family why the true cause must be written
exam_pearl: The words "treated completely" remove pneumonia from the certificate; without them, pneumonia gets recorded too.

stem: Patient With Lung cancer and pneumonia. The patient passed away and the doctor was going to write in the report that cancer is the cause of death but the patient family refused and insisted it was pneumonia, best action? (THEY DID NOT MENTION THAT PNEUMONIA WAS TREATED)
OptA: Write pneumonia as the cause of death
OptB: Write lung cancer as the cause of death
OptC: Write that pneumonia was a contributing factor to death
highlight_terms_source: THEY DID NOT MENTION THAT PNEUMONIA WAS TREATED
why_right: Here the stem does not say the pneumonia was treated, so it was presumably active at death and genuinely part of what killed the patient. The truthful record therefore keeps the lung cancer and also documents pneumonia as contributing, which is accurate and also addresses the family's concern without falsifying anything.
why_wrong_block:
A. Writing pneumonia alone hides the underlying lung cancer, the disease that set the chain of events in motion; that misrepresents the true cause.
B. Writing only lung cancer omits an active, relevant condition; it is the key when the pneumonia had been fully treated (see the treated version of this recall).
key_concept:
Record every condition that truly contributed to death; never omit or substitute to please family.
  • Underlying cause = the disease that started the chain (lung cancer)
  • Active pneumonia at death = recorded as well
  • Pneumonia treated and resolved = not recorded as a cause
  • Accuracy, not family preference, decides the wording
exam_pearl: Pair with the "treated completely" twin: treated pneumonia gives cancer only; untreated pneumonia gives cancer plus pneumonia as contributing.

stem: A 70-Year-Old Man With Terminal Lung Cancer Came To The ER Because Of Abdominal Obstruction. He Had Discussed DNR Previously But No Official Documentation Was Completed. He Develops Cardiac Arrest In The OR. What Is The Right Ethical Action?
OptB: Follow The Patient’s Wish And Do Not Resuscitate
OptC: Contact The Hospital Ethics Department
OptD: Contact The Family Regarding Their Wish
why_right: A DNR was "discussed previously but no official documentation was completed", so no valid DNR order exists. In an arrest, without a valid written order the default is full resuscitation; there is no time to verify verbal history, and an arrest in the OR is often reversible. Goals of care can be readdressed and documented afterwards.
why_wrong_block:
B. Withholding CPR requires a valid, documented DNR order; an undocumented discussion is not enough to act on during an arrest.
C. The ethics department cannot be consulted during a cardiac arrest; it suits non-urgent disputes about goals of care.
D. Calling the family wastes critical minutes and their wishes do not replace a documented order; involve them after the event to clarify and document goals.
key_concept:
No valid documented DNR = full resuscitation.
  • Valid DNR (documented, signed per policy) = do not resuscitate
  • Verbal or undocumented discussion = resuscitate
  • Emergency: act first, clarify goals of care and document afterwards
  • Ethics committee: non-urgent dilemmas only
exam_pearl: "Discussed but not documented" is the trap; only a documented DNR stops CPR.

stem: What is the primary approach that is used by the IRB to assess the ethical acceptability of a research study?
OptB: Deontology
OptC: Ethical skepticism
OptD: Comparativeism
highlight_terms_source: ethical acceptability of a research study
why_right: An IRB's central task is to weigh the risks against the expected benefits of a study (to participants and to society) and approve it only if the benefits justify the risks. That outcome-based, greatest-good weighing is a utilitarian approach, so this recall's key is utilitarianism.
why_wrong_block:
B. Deontology judges acts by duties and rules regardless of outcome; it underlies requirements like informed consent, but it is not the overall risk/benefit test the IRB applies.
C. Ethical skepticism doubts that moral knowledge is possible at all; it cannot provide a working standard for approving research.
D. Comparativeism is not a recognized framework for research ethics review; it is a distractor.
key_concept:
IRB approval = risks minimized and reasonable in relation to anticipated benefits.
  • Utilitarianism: judge by consequences, greatest good for the greatest number
  • Deontology: judge by duties/rules (consent, truth telling)
  • Virtue ethics: judge by the character of the agent
  • IRB also checks informed consent, privacy and fair participant selection
exam_pearl: "Risk/benefit balance" or "greatest good" in an ethics stem points to utilitarianism.

stem: A group of researchers doing research about children with diabetes in schools what is the primary approach that is used by the IRB to assess the ethical used of acceptability:
OptB: Subjectivism
key_concept:
IRB review = are risks minimized and justified by expected benefits?
  • Utilitarianism: consequences, greatest good (risk/benefit)
  • Deontology: duties and rules (consent, confidentiality)
  • Subjectivism: morality is personal opinion (not used by IRBs)
  • Research in children also needs parental permission and the child's assent
exam_pearl: If utilitarianism or "risk/benefit" appears in the real options, choose it.
