stem: A COPD patient with recorded Do Not Intubate (DNI) his case deteriorated. The team thinks intubating him might prolong his life. What would you do in this case?
OptB: Consult his family before making a decision
OptC: Proceed with intubation as it may prolong his life
OptD: Intubate the patient regardless of his DNI
why_right: The patient has a recorded DNI, which is his autonomous decision and stays binding when he deteriorates. The team's belief that intubation "might prolong his life" does not override a valid refusal, so the team respects the DNI and continues all other appropriate treatment and comfort care.
why_wrong_block:
B. The family cannot override a competent patient's documented decision; involving them for support is fine, but the decision is already made.
C. Prolonging life does not justify overriding a valid refusal of treatment; this would be right only if no DNI existed.
D. Intubating against a documented DNI violates autonomy and is battery; it would only be considered if the DNI were invalid or revoked by the patient.
key_concept:
A valid documented DNI/DNR is binding, even if the team disagrees.
  • Patient (or valid advance directive) decides, not family or team
  • DNI means no intubation, not no treatment
  • Oxygen, drugs, NIV and comfort care continue as per goals
  • No valid documentation = provide full treatment
exam_pearl: "Recorded" DNI = respect it; "discussed but not documented" = full treatment.

stem: Elderly women with progressive pulmonary fibrosis expresses wishe to do not intubate (DNI) and the patient signs the consent (she was conscious and alert) After that the pt deteriorate and started to develop respiratory distress, a nurse aims to help and the patient’s son want to intubate her regardless the DNI What should the nurse do ?
OptB: Endorracheal intubation
OptC: Do non invasive ventilation
OptD: Do not intubate because the pt signs the order
highlight_terms_source: patient’s son want to intubate her
why_right: She signed a DNI while "conscious and alert", so intubation is refused and the son cannot override it. But DNI means only no endotracheal intubation, not no treatment: her new respiratory distress can still be supported with non invasive ventilation, which respects her wish while actively helping her breathe.
why_wrong_block:
A. Palliative care alone fits a patient who has declined all life sustaining support or chosen comfort measures only; she refused intubation, not every treatment.
B. Intubation directly violates her valid, signed DNI; the son's wish does not override a competent patient's decision.
D. Not intubating is correct, but it is incomplete: it leaves her distress untreated when NIV is still allowed and can help.
key_concept:
DNI = no intubation; all other indicated treatment continues.
  • Allowed under DNI: oxygen, NIV, drugs, comfort care
  • Competent patient's signed directive overrides family requests
  • Family or son cannot consent to what the patient refused
  • DNR vs DNI: DNR = no CPR; DNI = no intubation
exam_pearl: "Do not intubate" is not "do nothing": choose the active treatment that stays inside the DNI.

stem: man and his wife decide to do IVF, and they did it and there is an embryo, they decide to get divorce before insering it inside the wife, so what should you do with embryo
OptA: Allow the husband to get it in a new wife
OptB: Gets rid of it
OptC: Allow the ex-wife to keep it with the consent from the husband
OptD: Froze it until The disagreement resolved
why_right: In Islamic and Saudi regulations, an embryo may be transferred only to the wife within a valid, existing marriage between the two gamete providers. Once the couple divorce (or the husband dies) before transfer, the marriage contract has ended, so the embryo cannot be implanted in anyone and is discarded.
why_wrong_block:
A. Placing the embryo in a new wife is third party involvement (a form of surrogacy), which is prohibited.
C. After divorce she is no longer his wife, so transfer is not permitted even with the ex-husband's consent.
D. Freezing to wait for a resolution does not help: the divorce, not a disagreement, is what makes transfer impermissible.
key_concept:
Assisted reproduction in Saudi practice is limited to a married couple using their own gametes during the marriage.
  • Divorce or husband's death before transfer = embryo cannot be transferred
  • Donor eggs, donor sperm, donor embryos = not permitted
  • Surrogacy (including a co-wife or new wife) = not permitted
  • Consent of both spouses needed for IVF steps
exam_pearl: The word "divorce" before transfer means the embryo is discarded; consent from either party does not change it.

stem: A married couple, both 35, married for 10 years and been trying to conceive. Both are fertile. Fertility induction and egg retrieval was successful. Before the next appointment for embryonic implantation, the couple got divorced. What do you do with the embryo?
OptA: Permit Husband to implant it in his new wife
OptB: Keep embryo and wait till legal settlement is done
OptC: Discard of embryo, since marital status is illegal.
OptD: Allow wife to use it after ex-husband’s consent
highlight_terms_source: Before the next appointment for embryonic implantation, the couple got divorced
why_right: In the Saudi/Islamic framework, assisted reproduction is allowed only between a husband and wife within a valid, ongoing marriage, using their own gametes. Once the couple got divorced before implantation, the marriage that made the embryo's use lawful has ended, so the embryo can no longer be transferred to either of them and is discarded.
why_wrong_block:
A. The embryo carries the ex-wife's egg, so transferring it to the husband's new wife means she gestates another woman's embryo (equivalent to egg donation or surrogacy), which is prohibited.
B. Waiting for a legal settlement does not help: no settlement can restore the marriage bond that the embryo's use depends on, and indefinite storage serves no lawful purpose.
D. The ex-husband's consent cannot make it lawful; after divorce they are no longer spouses, so transfer to the ex-wife is still prohibited. Consent matters only while the marriage exists.
key_concept:
IVF in Saudi practice: own gametes + husband and wife + marriage still valid at the time of transfer.
  • Divorce before transfer: embryos are not used (discarded)
  • Death of husband: stored sperm/embryos are not used
  • No donor eggs, donor sperm or surrogacy
  • Prior consent forms do not override the end of the marriage
exam_pearl: The trap is 'consent of the ex-spouse': consent is irrelevant once the marriage contract has ended.

stem: A pregnant woman presented to the clinic. During her visit the doctor informed her that the fetus has anencephaly and advised for termination. The wife agreed but her husband is refusing. What is the appropriate action?
OptA: You need both consent from her and husband
OptB: Only need her consent
OptC: Only need her consent and she should inform her husband
OptD: Obtain consent from a representative
highlight_terms_source: wife agreed but her husband is refusing
why_right: This is a termination for a fetal anomaly (anencephaly), not a procedure to save the mother's life. Under Saudi regulations, therapeutic termination in this setting requires the written consent of both the woman and her husband, so with the husband refusing the doctor cannot proceed on her consent alone; the couple should be counselled together.
why_wrong_block:
B. Her consent alone suffices for her own treatment (e.g., surgery for a miscarriage or a life threatening condition), but elective termination for fetal anomaly needs the husband's consent as well.
C. Simply informing the husband is not the same as obtaining his consent; the rule requires his agreement, not notification.
D. A representative consents only when the patient lacks capacity; here both spouses are competent and available.
key_concept:
Consent for pregnancy termination in Saudi practice:
  • Fetal anomaly (e.g., anencephaly): consent of both wife and husband
  • Mother's life in danger: treat to save her; her consent is what matters
  • Her own treatment (e.g., evacuation, laparotomy): competent woman signs for herself
  • Husband cannot sign instead of a competent wife
exam_pearl: Who signs for HER treatment = the patient; who must agree to TERMINATE a pregnancy for fetal anomaly = both spouses.

stem: A doctor agreed that the patient needs to abort the child due to chromosomal anomalies, but the father refused. What is the appropriate course of action in this situation?
OptB: Mother's consent prevails
OptC: Father's consent prevails
OptD: Consult ethics committee
why_right: This recall's key is that the father's refusal prevails. The reasoning: termination for a chromosomal anomaly (not a threat to the mother's life) needs the consent of both spouses under Saudi regulations, so when the father refused, the abortion cannot go ahead; in effect his refusal decides the outcome.
why_wrong_block:
A. The doctor's medical opinion does not replace consent; the doctor recommends, the patients decide.
B. The mother's consent alone is enough for her own treatment, but not for termination for a fetal anomaly, which also needs the husband's agreement.
D. An ethics committee helps when the rule is unclear or capacity is in doubt; here the regulation is clear (both consents needed), so it does not override the father's refusal.
key_concept:
Termination for fetal anomaly = joint consent; missing one consent means no termination.
  • Both agree: proceed per regulations
  • Either refuses: do not proceed, counsel the couple
  • Mother's life at risk: proceed to save her
exam_pearl: Read 'father's consent prevails' as 'without his consent it cannot be done', not that the father outranks the mother.

stem: In a case of anencephaly, the doctor advised an abortion. The mother agreed to the procedure, but the father refused. What is the most appropriate action?
OptB: Mothers decision prevails
OptC: Doctor decides
OptD: Consent taken from both mother and father
why_right: Termination for anencephaly is done for a fetal anomaly, not to save the mother's life, so Saudi regulations require consent from both the mother and the father. With the father refusing, the correct answer is to state the joint consent requirement and counsel the couple, not to let one side override the other.
why_wrong_block:
A. The father does not decide alone; his agreement is one of the two required consents, not a veto right over his wife's care in general.
B. The mother decides alone for her own treatment, or when her life is at risk; termination for fetal anomaly also requires the husband's consent.
C. The doctor gives the medical recommendation but cannot authorize a termination without the parents' consent.
key_concept:
Fetal anomaly termination: consent of wife + husband.
  • Her own surgery or evacuation: she signs
  • Life saving for the mother: proceed on her consent
  • Doctor never consents on the patient's behalf when she is competent
exam_pearl: If the question says 'anomaly' and one spouse refuses, the answer is joint consent; if it says 'her life is at risk', she decides.

stem: A woman underwent colectomy with good recovery. Upon discharge the doctor gave her 4 weeks of sick leave. She mentions that a friend who had the same surgery received 6 weeks of sick leave and requests an extension. What is the most appropriate response?
OptA: See her after 2 weeks to assess her recovery
OptB: Tell her the standard duration is 4 weeks
OptC: Give her 6 weeks of sick leave
OptD: Talk to her employer for longer sick leave
why_right: Sick leave must be based on the patient's own clinical condition, not on what another patient received. She had a good recovery, so the fair, professional response is to reassess her at follow up (after 2 weeks) and extend the leave only if her recovery actually requires it.
why_wrong_block:
B. Insisting on a fixed 'standard' duration ignores individual variation; leave should match her recovery, and the door to extension should stay open if clinically needed.
C. Granting 6 weeks because a friend got it is certifying leave without a medical reason, which is dishonest documentation.
D. Negotiating with her employer breaches confidentiality and is not the doctor's role; the doctor certifies medical fitness only.
key_concept:
Sick leave requests: decide on clinical grounds, reassess, document honestly.
  • Never issue leave on comparison or pressure
  • Reassess at follow up and extend if recovery is slow
  • Do not contact employers without consent
exam_pearl: 'Friend got more' is not an indication; the answer is reassessment, not refusal or automatic extension.

stem: A pregnant woman in active labor presents with signs of obstructed labor and fetal distress. She is counseled for an emergency cesarean section but she refuses the procedure and requests a second opinion. What is the most appropriate next step in managing this situation?
OptB: Try to persuade her with CS against her will
OptC: Respect her refusal and request for a second opinion
OptD: Consent from both the mother and father is required before proceeding
highlight_terms_source: refuses the procedure and requests a second opinion
why_right: A competent woman who has been counselled has the right to refuse a cesarean section, even with fetal distress and obstructed labour; maternal autonomy overrides fetal interest. She has also asked for a second opinion, which is reasonable and should be arranged promptly while monitoring continues and her refusal is documented.
why_wrong_block:
A. The husband (father) cannot consent on behalf of a competent adult woman; his consent is not a substitute for hers.
B. Proceeding against her will is coercion and assault; persuasion may continue through counselling, but surgery cannot be done without her consent.
D. Joint spousal consent applies to things like termination for fetal anomaly, not to a competent woman's own surgery; and here she has refused, so no one else's consent changes that.
key_concept:
Competent pregnant woman refusing CS:
  • Explain risks clearly, confirm capacity
  • Respect refusal, document informed refusal
  • Arrange a second opinion promptly if requested
  • Continue best care within her consent (e.g., vaginal delivery, monitoring)
  • No husband consent, no court order, no sedation
exam_pearl: Fetal distress makes CS indicated, not mandatory: the competent mother still decides.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Two more versions in the block agree: (Q:) 42-week pregnant woman, CTG fetal distress, refuses CS and requests second opinion: B. Respect her wishes and wait for the second opinion [highlighted]. (Q:) Patient couldn't deliver vaginally, fetus in distress, refused CS and wanted second opinion: C. wait for second opinion [highlighted].

stem: A pregnant woman in labor is told that a vaginal delivery is dangerous for the fetus and a C-section is necessary. The patient understands the risks but refuses the surgery and insists on a vaginal delivery. What should the doctor do?
OptA: Refer her to the psychiatric department.
OptB: Sedate her and perform the C-section.
OptC: Respect her decision.
OptD: Obtain consent from her husband
highlight_terms_source: understands the risks but refuses the surgery
why_right: The woman understands the risks and still refuses the surgery, which shows capacity. A competent adult may refuse a cesarean even if the fetus may not survive; the doctor respects her decision, documents the informed refusal, and continues to support a safe vaginal delivery while remaining ready if she changes her mind.
why_wrong_block:
A. Psychiatric referral is for doubts about capacity (e.g., psychosis, inability to understand); disagreeing with the doctor is not a sign of incapacity.
B. Sedating her to operate is forced treatment and assault; it is never acceptable in a competent patient.
D. The husband cannot consent for a competent wife's own surgery; her refusal stands.
key_concept:
Informed refusal by a competent pregnant woman = respect it.
  • Capacity: understands, retains, weighs, communicates
  • Psychiatry only if capacity is genuinely doubtful
  • No husband consent, court order or sedation to override
  • Document and keep offering care
exam_pearl: 'Understands the risks' in the stem confirms capacity, so the answer is to respect her decision.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot on next page of the same concept: 27-year-old in last trimester with severe cephalopelvic disproportion refuses CS; fully understands; fetus may not survive. Options: a. Honor her wishes and do not perform the C-section, b. Psychiatry evaluation, c. Sedate her and perform the surgery, d. Obtain a court order, e. Explain to the baby's father and ask him for consent. Answer: (a) Honor her wishes and do not perform the C-section.

stem: A couple undergoing infertility treatment with IVF. During the procedure, the husband died. What is the appropriate management of the sperm samples stored in the laboratory?
OptA: Obtain consent from the husband’s family
OptB: Discard the sperm samples
OptC: Allow the wife to continue the procedure if a prior written consent exists
OptD: Missed
why_right: In the Saudi/Islamic framework, gametes and embryos may be used only between a husband and wife while the marriage is valid. The husband died during IVF, which ends the marriage, so his stored sperm cannot be used to inseminate the widow and the samples are discarded.
why_wrong_block:
A. The family has no authority over his gametes, and their consent cannot make posthumous use lawful.
C. Prior written consent allows posthumous use in some Western jurisdictions, but not in Saudi practice, where the end of the marriage ends any permitted use.
D. This option was not recalled by the source, so it cannot be assessed.
key_concept:
Posthumous reproduction is not permitted in Saudi practice.
  • Husband dies: stored sperm and embryos are not used
  • Divorce: same rule
  • Consent forms or family wishes do not change it
exam_pearl: 'Prior written consent' is the Western answer and the trap here.

stem: Infetile couple came for Ivf in the mid of the process, the husband dies, embryo is there The mother want to proceed and get pregnant Best action?
OptA: She can’t since the husband is dead
OptB: She can since the consent of the couple was taken
why_right: The husband died in the middle of IVF, so the marriage that permitted use of the couple's embryo has ended. In Saudi/Islamic practice the widow cannot have the embryo transferred, even though the couple originally consented together.
why_wrong_block: B. The couple's earlier consent was given for treatment within a living marriage; it does not extend past the husband's death, so it cannot authorise transfer now.
key_concept:
Embryo/sperm use requires a living, valid marriage at the time of use.
  • Husband dead or divorced: do not transfer, embryos discarded
  • Earlier joint consent does not survive death or divorce
exam_pearl: 'Consent was taken from the couple' sounds right but is the trap: the marriage, not the form, is what matters.

stem: A 50 year old female with a history of severe multiple sclerosis was recently diagnosed ESRD. The patient is alert and has expressed a wish for "Do Not Resuscitate" (DNR). A recent lab result shows a potassium level of 6. What is the appropriate action?
OptA: Dialysis is possible after reversal of DNR
OptB: Dialysis cannot be done because of DNR
OptC: Ignore the patient's wishes and proceed with dialysis
OptD: Give kayxzine and discuss DNR with the family
why_right: The decisive point is that a DNR order covers only cardiopulmonary resuscitation after arrest; it is not a 'do not treat' order. This alert patient now has ESRD with hyperkalemia ("potassium level of 6"), and dialysis is the definitive, life-saving treatment for hyperkalemia in ESRD. The recall's key means: do not let the DNR block dialysis, proceed with indicated treatment.
why_wrong_block:
A. There is no need to reverse the DNR first; DNR and dialysis are independent decisions, so the DNR can stay in place while she is dialysed.
B. Wrong interpretation of DNR: it withholds CPR only, not other indicated treatments such as dialysis, antibiotics or surgery.
D. She is alert and competent, so the DNR is her decision, not the family's; and a potassium binder alone is a temporizing measure, not definitive therapy for hyperkalemia in ESRD.
key_concept:
DNR = no CPR on arrest; every other indicated treatment continues.
  • DNR does not mean withhold dialysis, antibiotics, fluids or surgery
  • Competent patient: code status decided with the patient, not the family
  • Hyperkalemia in ESRD: definitive treatment is dialysis
  • Binders and shifting agents only buy time
exam_pearl: Trap: treating 'DNR' as 'do not treat'; it only removes CPR from the plan.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant in same block: 48-year-old diabetic with advanced progressive MS, renal failure secondary to diabetes, alert, elected DNR at her own discretion, potassium 8 (high); options same; 'Ignore DNR and start dialysis' highlighted.

stem: Female newly married she was using OCP before marriage, her husband want her to stop taking ocp because he wants to start family immediately, but the wife refused, what to do?
OptA: There should be a medical reasons
OptB: The husband has the top priority in absence of medical reasons
highlight_terms_source: husband want her to stop taking ocp
why_right: This recall's key reflects the view that, within marriage, the husband's wish to start a family is given weight when there is no medical reason for the wife to avoid pregnancy. The stem gives no medical contraindication to pregnancy ("newly married", healthy, using OCP before marriage), so the key applies the 'absence of medical reasons' rule.
why_wrong_block: A. A medical reason (a condition that makes pregnancy unsafe) is what would justify continuing contraception against the husband's wish; the stem describes none, so this option does not settle the case.
key_concept:
Spouses disagree on contraception: this recall keys the husband's wish when there is no medical reason to avoid pregnancy.
  • Medical contraindication to pregnancy: continuing contraception is justified (option A's point)
  • No medical reason (this stem): the key gives the husband's wish priority
  • Other versions of this question key 'mutual consent required', with the doctor counselling the couple together
  • A competent adult woman consents to her own treatment; the husband cannot sign for her
exam_pearl: Other versions of this question key 'mutual consent required', not siding with either spouse.

stem: A doctor prescribed a drug for a child and miscalculated the patient’s weight, causing side effects. How can this be prevented?
OptB: Use standardized protocols based on the patient’s weight
OptC: Calculate based on the patient’s age
OptD: Let the nurse adjust the medication if she experiences side effects
why_right: This is a pediatric weight-based dosing error, and the question asks how to prevent it. Prevention is a system fix: standardized weight-based protocols (dosing charts, accurate recorded weight, double checks) remove reliance on individual calculation. Children's doses are calculated per kilogram, so the safeguard must be built around weight.
why_wrong_block:
A. Concentrated formulations make small calculation slips more dangerous (tenfold errors); safety practice favors standard, lower concentrations.
C. Age is a poor surrogate for body size; pediatric drugs are dosed by weight, so switching to age-based dosing adds error.
D. This reacts after harm has occurred rather than preventing it, and a nurse should not change a prescribed dose on her own.
key_concept:
Medication error prevention = system-level standardization, not individual vigilance.
  • Pediatric dosing: per kg, using an accurately measured weight
  • Standard protocols and dosing charts
  • Standard concentrations
  • Independent double check of high-risk drugs
exam_pearl: 'How to prevent' questions want a system solution (protocols), not a reactive or individual fix.

stem: Female pt. With history of anxiety disorder. came with lethargy fatigue and want some days off. She said she is in a stressful time but there is no physical symptoms What ethical point?
OptB: Don’t give her
OptC: Refer to stress management and don’t give
why_right: A sick leave certificate must reflect a doctor's judgement that the patient is medically unfit to work. Here she reports a "stressful time" with "no physical symptoms" and asks for days off; issuing leave on request alone is inaccurate certification. This recall's key addresses the real problem by referring her for stress management instead of granting the leave.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sick leave is right only if assessment shows her condition (for example an anxiety exacerbation) actually makes her unfit to work, not simply because she asks.
B. Refusing without offering any help for her stress and known anxiety disorder abandons her care; C pairs the refusal with support.
key_concept:
Medical certificates must be truthful and based on clinical assessment.
  • Request without objective unfitness: do not certify
  • Address the underlying problem (stress, anxiety) with appropriate referral
  • Mental illness causing functional impairment can justify leave
exam_pearl: Never issue sick leave just because the patient asks; certify only genuine medical unfitness.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler note: 'C/A??' (unsure between C and A).
Other marked answers: Compiler note 'C/A??': A

stem: Post surgery Sickleave - her relative take 6 week and the doctor prescribe her only 4 she asked more even with sign of recovery were found what to do?
OptA: follow up with 2 week to assure recovery
OptB: Recommend to ask employed for more leave if poor recovery
OptC: Standard is 4 weeks
why_right: Sick leave length is set by the individual patient's recovery, not by what a relative received. She already shows "signs of recovery", so extending leave now is not justified; arranging a review in 2 weeks lets the doctor reassess and extend only if recovery is actually incomplete.
why_wrong_block:
B. Sick leave is a medical decision made by the treating doctor; telling her to negotiate with her employer shifts that responsibility away from the clinical assessment.
C. There is no fixed universal duration; quoting a 'standard' dismisses her concern without a plan to reassess.
key_concept:
Sick leave is individualized, evidence-based and reviewed.
  • Base duration on clinical recovery, not comparison with others
  • Recovering well: do not extend on request
  • Doubt about recovery: schedule review and extend if needed
exam_pearl: Another patient's leave is irrelevant; reassess this patient's recovery at follow-up.

stem: A 60-year-old man with bowel obstruction requires hospital admission but refuses despite medical advice, What is the best action?
OptA: Force him to stay as he may be psychotic
OptB: Let him sign a DAMA form
OptC: Ensure that he understands the risks and allow him to sign discharge papers
OptD: Call security to restrain the patient
why_right: A competent adult may refuse admission even when the condition ("bowel obstruction") is serious. The doctor must first make sure the refusal is informed: he understands the risks, including death, and has capacity. Only then is discharge against medical advice signed and documented, which is why C is better than simply handing him a form.
why_wrong_block:
A. Refusing advice is not evidence of psychosis; capacity is presumed and must be assessed, not assumed absent. Holding him is right only if he truly lacks capacity.
B. Signing a DAMA form without first confirming he understands the risks is incomplete; the informed refusal step is what C adds.
D. Restraining a competent adult is battery; security and restraint are for patients lacking capacity who are a danger, or for public health threats such as Ebola.
key_concept:
Patient wants to leave: capacity, informed refusal, then DAMA with documentation.
  • Explain risks and alternatives, confirm understanding
  • Document refusal, sign DAMA
  • Give instructions and an open door to return
  • Exceptions: lacks capacity, notifiable infection (Ebola), suspected child abuse
exam_pearl: Between 'sign DAMA' and 'ensure he understands, then sign', pick the one that includes informed refusal.

stem: Patient admitted as a case of severe pneumonia and 2 days after initiating Abx he started feeling slighty better and decided to leave the hospital against medical advice, what should the physician do?
OptA: Call security and stop him from leaving
OptB: Allow him to leave without documented
OptC: Respect autonomy, sign DAMA , give instructions
highlight_terms_source: leave the hospital against medical advice
why_right: He is a competent adult who is "feeling slightly better" and chooses to leave; autonomy must be respected. The correct process is to explain the risks, have him sign discharge against medical advice, and give follow-up instructions (complete antibiotics, warning signs, return at any time). Pneumonia is not a public health threat that justifies detention.
why_wrong_block:
A. Detaining a competent patient is not allowed; security is reserved for patients lacking capacity who are dangerous, or contagious notifiable diseases such as Ebola.
B. Letting him go without documentation leaves no record of informed refusal and no safety instructions; DAMA must always be documented.
key_concept:
DAMA package: explain risks, document, sign, give instructions, keep the door open.
  • Competent adult: respect autonomy
  • Ensure treatment continues as far as possible (oral antibiotics, follow-up)
  • Detain only if no capacity, or public health threat (Ebola)
exam_pearl: Ordinary pneumonia leaving AMA = DAMA; Ebola leaving = call security.

stem: Patient tested positive for Ebola and asked treating physician to either discharge him or let him leave the hospital. What is the correct action?
OptB: Consult ethics committee
OptC: Refer to infectious disease
OptD: Make him sign discharge against medical advice
why_right: He "tested positive for Ebola", a highly contagious, notifiable disease. When a patient's leaving endangers the public, public safety overrides individual autonomy, so he must not be allowed to leave isolation and hospital security is called to prevent it. Infection control and public health authorities are then involved.
why_wrong_block:
B. An ethics consult is for genuine dilemmas and takes time; isolation of an Ebola case is mandatory, and the immediate need is to stop him leaving now.
C. He is already under treatment; an infectious disease referral does not address the urgent risk of him walking out.
D. DAMA applies when refusal harms only the patient; releasing an Ebola case would expose the community.
key_concept:
Autonomy ends where the patient's choice endangers others.
  • Ebola or similar notifiable contagious disease refusing isolation: call security, prevent leaving
  • Suspected child abuse with parents leaving: report and keep the child
  • Ordinary illness, competent adult: DAMA
exam_pearl: Contagious notifiable disease flips the usual DAMA answer to 'call security'.

stem: a patient have to do open heart surgery, He wanted to sign DAMA and refuses the surgery, because he wanted to go back home and use traditional/herbal “something like that” medication to treat his condition. What to do?
OptA: Discuss ethics committee, document his refusal, and advice him
OptB: explain the risk, urge him to stay, then let him go (No mention of DAMA documentation in that option)
OptC: let him go
OptD: don’t let him go
highlight_terms_source: sign DAMA and refuses the surgery
why_right: A competent adult may refuse even life-saving "open heart surgery" in favor of herbal treatment. The key combines what is required: document the refusal, keep advising him (risks, and that he can return), and use institutional support such as the ethics committee when a refusal carries grave consequences. The refusal is respected but handled properly.
why_wrong_block:
B. Explaining and urging are correct, but letting him go without documenting the refusal is a medicolegal failure; documentation is mandatory.
C. Simply letting him go skips explanation of risks, informed refusal and documentation.
D. Preventing a competent adult from leaving violates autonomy; detention is only for lack of capacity or public health threats.
key_concept:
Competent refusal of major surgery: respect it, but inform, document and keep counselling.
  • Confirm capacity and understanding of risks
  • Document refusal (DAMA)
  • Continue to advise; leave the door open to return
  • Spouse or family cannot override a competent adult
exam_pearl: The option that includes documentation of refusal beats one that only explains and lets him go.

stem: 74 years old with pulmonary fibrosis presented to ER with multiple respiratory failure episodes, the patient expressed desire to DNI and signed it, then presented again the respiratory distress, the nurse go to case but her doughter wanted to intubate her to prolong her life, what should the nurse do?
OptB: stop respiratory support due DNI
OptC: proceed with intubation
OptD: non invasive respiratory
why_right: She "signed" a DNI while competent, so intubation is excluded and her daughter cannot override it. DNI forbids only intubation; it does not mean stopping all treatment. Non-invasive ventilation is a reasonable ceiling of support that respects her directive while still treating the respiratory distress.
why_wrong_block:
A. Comfort-only care goes beyond what she requested; DNI limits intubation, not every active treatment. It would be right if she had chosen comfort care only.
B. Withdrawing all respiratory support wrongly expands DNI into 'do not treat'.
C. Intubating violates the competent patient's documented DNI; a family member's wish does not override the patient's own directive.
key_concept:
Code status orders are specific: honor exactly what was declined.
  • DNR: no CPR
  • DNI: no intubation, other support (NIV, oxygen, drugs) allowed
  • Comfort care only: a separate, explicit decision
  • Family cannot override a competent patient's directive
exam_pearl: DNI is not 'do not treat'; NIV remains available.

stem: A young girl has been experiencing severe symptoms of depression and has made multiple suicide attempts. The doctor recommends that she be admitted to the hospital for her safety. However, the girl becomes very upset and angry about this decision. What ethical principle is guiding the doctor's recommendation to admit her?
OptB: Beneficence
OptC: Nonmaleficence
OptD: Autonomy?
highlight_terms_source: admitted to the hospital for her safety
why_right: The doctor is acting to do good and protect the patient: "severe depression" with "multiple suicide attempts" means a high, real risk of death, and admission "for her safety" is a positive step taken in her best interest. Acting to promote the patient's welfare and prevent harm to her is beneficence. Her anger shows the doctor is placing her welfare above her stated wishes, which is beneficence outweighing autonomy when capacity and safety are in question.
why_wrong_block:
A. Justice is about fair distribution of resources and treating similar patients equally (e.g. bed allocation, triage); nothing here concerns fairness between patients.
C. Nonmaleficence means avoiding harm caused by the doctor's own actions (e.g. not giving a harmful drug). Admission is an active intervention to benefit her, which is beneficence; nonmaleficence is the answer when the question is about withholding a harmful intervention.
D. Autonomy would favour her wish not to be admitted; the doctor is overriding that wish, so autonomy is the principle being limited, not the one guiding the decision.
key_concept:
Beneficence = act in the patient's best interest (do good); nonmaleficence = do no harm.
  • Admitting a suicidal patient for safety: beneficence
  • Avoiding a harmful or futile intervention: nonmaleficence
  • Respecting a competent patient's choice: autonomy
  • Fair allocation of resources: justice
  • Previous attempts and social isolation are strong suicide risk factors
exam_pearl: If the doctor is DOING something to help the patient against her wishes, think beneficence; if the doctor is AVOIDING something harmful, think nonmaleficence.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Options C and D are run together on the page ('NonmaleficenceD-Autonomy?').

stem: A female presents with weight loss. A biopsy is performed, and the results confirm ovarian cancer. What is the best way to break the bad news to the patient?
OptA: “I have some serious news. Can we talk about it?”
OptB: “We found a mass, it could be cancer.”
OptC: “Don't worry about it; everything will be fine
why_right: Breaking bad news follows SPIKES: prepare the setting, check what the patient knows, ask for her invitation, and give a warning shot before the knowledge. "I have some serious news. Can we talk about it?" does exactly this: it signals that bad news is coming and asks permission to continue, letting the patient prepare. The confirmed biopsy ("results confirm ovarian cancer") is then explained clearly, followed by empathy and a plan.
why_wrong_block:
B. "We found a mass, it could be cancer" is abrupt (no warning shot or invitation) and inaccurate, because the biopsy has already confirmed cancer; vague hedging is only appropriate before a tissue diagnosis exists.
C. "Don't worry, everything will be fine" is false reassurance: it withholds the diagnosis, is dishonest and blocks informed decisions about treatment.
key_concept:
SPIKES for breaking bad news:
  • S: Setting, private room, time, support person
  • P: Perception, what does she already know?
  • I: Invitation, how much does she want to know?
  • K: Knowledge, warning shot then clear, jargon free facts
  • E: Emotions, respond with empathy
  • S: Strategy and summary, plan and follow up
exam_pearl: The best opening line is a warning shot plus a request for permission; blunt facts or false reassurance are always wrong.

stem: Researcher wants to apply for a IRB but the ethics authority have concerns and reject it. He will search about best cervical cancer screening method . The concern is that the patients will not know cervical screening guidelines nor the results of the screening ( positive or negative ) . What will help get his application accepted ?
OptB: Send reports to the patients with high alarm systems
OptC: Tell the negative cases about their results
OptD: Call positive cases about their results and instruct them where to go after that.
why_right: The ethics committee rejected the protocol because participants would "not know" their screening results. A study that detects disease must have a plan to disclose clinically significant results and link participants to care; otherwise it exposes them to harm without benefit. Calling the positive cases and telling them "where to go after that" (referral for colposcopy and treatment) directly fixes the concern, which is what makes the application acceptable.
why_wrong_block:
A. The committee has already raised a valid concern; resubmitting unchanged will not be accepted because withholding actionable results breaches beneficence and the duty of care to participants.
B. Sending alarming reports without counselling or a referral pathway causes anxiety and does not ensure follow up; results should be communicated in a supportive, actionable way.
C. Telling only the negative cases leaves the participants who actually need care uninformed, which is the opposite of what the committee requires.
key_concept:
Research ethics: participants with clinically significant findings must be informed and referred.
  • IRB protects participants: consent, confidentiality, risk minimisation
  • Screening study: plan for disclosure of positive results plus a referral pathway
  • Abnormal Pap or HPV result is triaged per guideline, often to colposcopy and biopsy
  • Disclosure should be by a clinician, with counselling, not an alarming report
exam_pearl: When a study finds disease, the fix is always disclosure to the positive participants plus a clear referral pathway.

stem: 1st trimester scan shows severe fetal anomaly mother requesting abortion. which should be considered?
OptB: societal interest
OptC: maternal autonomy
OptD: physician’s personal beliefs
why_right: The decision concerns the mother's own body and pregnancy, so the principle to respect is maternal autonomy: a competent, informed woman who "requests" termination after a "severe fetal anomaly" on a first trimester scan has her informed choice considered, within the legal framework (in Saudi Arabia this requires the conditions and medical committee approval set by regulation). The doctor counsels her on the findings, prognosis and options, then supports her informed decision rather than imposing outside interests.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fetal rights are weighed later in pregnancy and in the legal limits on termination, but they do not override an informed mother's decision in this scenario; they would be the focus if termination were requested late with a healthy fetus.
B. Societal interest is relevant to public health policy and resource decisions, not to an individual woman's decision about her own pregnancy.
D. The physician's personal beliefs must not drive the patient's care; a doctor with a conscientious objection should refer, not impose his beliefs.
key_concept:
Patient requesting a lawful intervention for herself: respect autonomy after full counselling.
  • Counsel: diagnosis, prognosis, options, risks
  • Decision belongs to the competent, informed woman within the law
  • Physician's personal beliefs: never imposed; conscientious objector refers
  • Detailed anomaly scan is at 18 to 22 weeks; first trimester findings may need confirmation
exam_pearl: Options naming the doctor's beliefs or society's interest are distractors; the competent patient's informed choice is the ethical anchor.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Another version: 'Pregnant, (1st visit at the antenatal clinic I think) with 14w want to terminate the pregnancy because of the anomaly' A- Respect the Autonomy, B- refuse, C- something like community ethics (no answer marked).

stem: Pregnant with 14w want to terminate the pregnancy for social reasons
OptB: refuse
OptC: sothing like community ethics
key_concept:
Autonomy = right to refuse and to choose among lawful, indicated options; it does not compel a doctor to provide an intervention that is unlawful or not indicated.
  • Competent patient refuses treatment: respect and document
  • Patient demands non-indicated or unlawful intervention: decline, explain, keep caring
  • Social reasons alone, beyond early pregnancy: not a lawful indication in Saudi Arabia
exam_pearl: Refusal of treatment = autonomy wins; demand for an unlawful or non-indicated procedure = the doctor may decline.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Pt pregnant and has disease and pregnancy risky for her life and doctor decide to abortion but parents refuse?
OptB: Respect parents wishes
why_right: This recall's key is to respect the refusal: termination is a major, irreversible intervention that cannot be performed without valid consent, and here consent has been withheld ("parents refuse"). The source's reasoning is that the doctor cannot proceed against the refusal; instead he explains the risk to her life, documents the discussion and keeps offering care. The stem is incomplete, so whose consent applies (patient vs guardians) is the deciding issue.
why_wrong_block: A. Aborting despite refusal means operating without valid consent; the source key does not accept this. It would be right if the patient herself (competent) consented, or in a true emergency where no one able to consent is available and delay would cost her life.
key_concept:
Consent rules for procedures:
  • Competent adult: she alone consents or refuses; husband or parents cannot substitute
  • Minor or patient lacking capacity: legal guardian consents
  • Competent refusal is respected even if life threatening, and documented
  • Life threatening emergency with no one able to consent: proceed with life saving treatment
exam_pearl: Always ask whose consent counts: a competent adult patient's own decision overrides any relative's.

stem: Pregnant woman with abdominal pain and doctor ordered abdominal ray for her after she done the ray the doctor realized that she was pregnant, how prevent this error?
OptB: Order US
OptC: Detect fetal age
why_right: This recall's key is to determine fetal (gestational) age: radiation risk to the fetus depends mainly on gestational age at exposure and dose, so knowing the age of the pregnancy is what guides whether ionising imaging is acceptable and how to counsel her. The broader safety rule is that every woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain has her pregnancy status checked before X-ray, and pregnancy, once known, is factored in before imaging.
why_wrong_block:
A. Proceeding with ionising imaging without first establishing pregnancy status and gestation is exactly how this error happened; it is acceptable only when the imaging is essential and the risk has been weighed.
B. Ultrasound avoids radiation and is the preferred first imaging in pregnancy, but it does not address the error itself, which was not knowing she was pregnant (and how far along) before the X-ray was ordered.
key_concept:
Radiation in women of reproductive age:
  • Ask about LMP and do a pregnancy test (beta hCG) before ionising imaging
  • Fetal risk depends on gestational age at exposure and dose
  • Prefer ultrasound or MRI when pregnant
  • Essential imaging should not be withheld; keep the dose as low as possible
  • After accidental exposure: determine gestational age and dose, then counsel
exam_pearl: The real prevention step is a pregnancy test before any X-ray in a woman of reproductive age.

stem: A patient had appendectomy and then developed an infection as a complication. There was a nurse from another department who is a family friend. She opened the file of the patient to see why she got the infection as to "check on her". The patient found out and filed a complaint. What's the proper action?
OptB: train the staff on confidentiality and privacy
OptC: inform patient and document
OptD: investigation and take a legal action
highlight_terms_source: opened the file of the patient
why_right: A nurse with no role in the patient's care opened the file out of personal curiosity ("to check on her"): this is unauthorised access and a breach of confidentiality, regardless of good intentions or being a family friend. The patient has made a formal complaint, so the hospital must investigate and apply disciplinary or legal action according to policy and the law.
why_wrong_block:
A. Dismissing a confirmed privacy breach and a formal complaint is never acceptable; it fails the patient and the institution's legal duty.
B. Staff training on confidentiality is a useful preventive measure afterwards, but it does not deal with this specific breach and complaint; it is the answer when asked how to prevent future breaches.
C. The patient already knows and has complained; documentation alone without investigation and accountability leaves the breach unaddressed. Informing and documenting is the answer for disclosing a complication or error.
key_concept:
Only staff directly involved in care may access a patient's record.
  • Family friend, curiosity or "checking on her": still a breach
  • Complaint of a breach: investigate, then disciplinary or legal action
  • Preventing future breaches: training and access audits
  • Relatives asking about a competent adult's condition: refer them to the patient
exam_pearl: Good intentions do not make unauthorised record access acceptable; a filed complaint calls for investigation and action.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-2443).
Compiler note: Number 991 printed at bottom of page 248; the screenshot is at the top of page 249 with 'Answer: D'.

stem: Elderly female patient with cancer who informed the nurse before losing consciousness that she did not wish to be resuscitated or receive further treatment. After she lost consciousness, her sons are now insisting on proceeding with resuscitation and treatment despite her prior wishes. What is the most appropriate course of action?
OptA: Respect her previously wishes and do not perform resuscitation.
OptB: Do the treatment as her son insists or something like that
highlight_terms_source: informed the nurse before losing consciousness
did not wish to be resuscitated
why_right: While competent, the patient clearly told the nurse she "did not wish to be resuscitated or receive further treatment". A competent patient's informed refusal remains valid after she "lost consciousness", so her previously expressed wishes are respected and resuscitation is not performed. Relatives cannot override a competent adult's prior decision; the team documents her wishes and continues comfort care.
why_wrong_block: B. The sons' insistence does not override the patient's own prior refusal; family wishes guide decisions only when the patient's own wishes are unknown and she lacks capacity.
key_concept:
Prior wishes of a competent patient bind after she loses capacity.
  • Competent refusal (including DNR) is respected and documented
  • Family cannot override the patient's known wishes
  • Wishes unknown: decide in her best interest with the medical team
  • Comfort and palliative care continue
exam_pearl: Known wishes of the patient beat family demands; family input matters only when her wishes are unknown.

stem: A couple came to the clinic due to primary infertility, IVF went successfully but there was excess amount of cryopreserved sperm what to do about it? )not exact citation but same concept
OptA: Keep it for use for indefinite time
OptB: Its prohibited ethically and religiously
OptC: Keep it for a specific time frame then ethically discard it
OptD: Keep it in a government-authorized fertility center
why_right: Surplus cryopreserved gametes after successful IVF are stored under a defined, regulated time limit agreed in the couple's consent, then disposed of ethically when that period ends or the couple no longer needs them. In the Saudi and Islamic framework they belong to the married couple and may be used only by them within the marriage, so they are never kept indefinitely or passed to others.
why_wrong_block:
A. Indefinite storage is not permitted: it raises the risk of use after divorce or death and of misuse outside the marriage, so storage must have a limit.
B. Cryopreservation of a married couple's own gametes for their own future use is permitted, so it is not prohibited; what is prohibited is use by third parties (donation or surrogacy).
D. Storage must be in a licensed centre, but this option omits the key point, a fixed storage period followed by ethical disposal.
key_concept:
Gamete and embryo storage: couple's own use, fixed time limit, then ethical disposal.
  • Used only by the married couple during the marriage
  • Donation of sperm, eggs or embryos and surrogacy: not permitted in Saudi Arabia
  • Divorce or death of a spouse: stored gametes are not used
  • Storage in a licensed centre under written consent
exam_pearl: "Indefinite" storage is the trap; the answer always has a time limit and ethical disposal.

stem: 20s years old female nurse called emergency dispatch and complained about Major depression disorder symptoms including suicidal ideation, discontinued her medications, what is the best step to ensure confidentiality?
OptA: Discuss her case with the mental health team
OptB: Ask colleague for their input
OptC: Tell her employer
OptD: Document the information and call her family immediately
why_right: She has suicidal ideation and has stopped her medications, so she needs urgent psychiatric care, but her information must stay within the people directly treating her. Sharing with the mental health team is a disclosure on a need to know basis inside the circle of care: it gets her the help she needs while keeping her confidentiality intact.
why_wrong_block:
B. Asking a colleague who is not involved in her care spreads her information beyond the treating team for no clinical gain. Consultation is fine only when that colleague is part of the care plan or details are anonymised.
C. Telling her employer is a clear breach; being a nurse does not entitle the employer to her psychiatric details. Occupational disclosure is considered only through formal fitness to practise routes when there is a real risk to patients, not as a first step.
D. Calling the family immediately discloses her condition to third parties without her consent. Family involvement is considered with her agreement, or without it only when disclosure is needed to prevent serious harm that the care team cannot otherwise manage.
key_concept:
Confidentiality: share the minimum necessary, with those directly involved in care.
  • Treating team (mental health team): appropriate sharing
  • Uninvolved colleagues: not appropriate
  • Employer, family: only with consent or a legal/serious risk justification
  • Suicide risk: urgent referral to psychiatry, not public disclosure
exam_pearl: "Ensure confidentiality" plus suicide risk = refer within the care team, not tell family or employer.

stem: Female with depression admitted for for non-controlled HTN due to non-adherence to
OptA: Share psychiatric history with the medical team
OptB: Ask colleague for their input
OptC: Tell her employer
OptD: Share mental history with the medical team that would be relevant to treatment
why_right: She is admitted for uncontrolled HTN from non adherence, and her depression may explain the non adherence, so the medical team does need to know about it. The principle is minimum necessary disclosure: share only the parts of her mental health history that are relevant to her current treatment.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sharing her whole psychiatric history goes beyond what the medical team needs; it is close but not the best answer. Full disclosure would be right only if all of it bears on the current management or she consents to it.
B. Asking an uninvolved colleague spreads her information outside the treating team and does not answer what should be shared. It is appropriate only for anonymised advice or when the colleague joins her care.
C. Telling her employer is a breach of confidentiality with no clinical justification. Disclosure to an employer requires her consent or a formal legal requirement.
key_concept:
Within the treating team, share what is relevant to care, not everything.
  • Relevant (depression driving non adherence): share
  • Unrelated psychiatric detail: withhold
  • Outside the team (employer, colleagues not involved): needs consent
exam_pearl: Two "share with the team" options: pick the one limited to what is relevant to treatment.

stem: A teenager with acne is treated with retinoids. The physician wants to post before-and-after photos on TikTok. What is the most appropriate action?
OptB: No consent needed if the patient is not identifiable
OptC: Posting is acceptable due to educational benefit
why_right: Clinical photographs are part of the medical record, and putting them on TikTok is a public use that needs explicit consent for that purpose. Because the patient is a teenager, this means consent from the legal guardian together with the patient's own agreement. Educational value never replaces consent.
why_wrong_block:
B. Before and after acne photos usually show the face and are easily identifiable; even truly de-identified images for public social media still require consent. Removing identifiers matters for internal teaching, not as a substitute for permission to post publicly.
C. Educational benefit does not override the patient's right to control use of his own images. Education justifies posting only after consent is obtained.
key_concept:
Patient images: consent first, for the specific use.
  • Public or social media posting: explicit consent for that purpose
  • Minor: guardian consent plus patient assent
  • De-identification: still needed, but not a replacement for consent
exam_pearl: "Educational" or "not identifiable" are traps; social media use of patient photos always needs consent.

stem: Patient is scheduled for a laparoscopic appendectomy in a private hospital. The doctor explained all the steps of the procedure and the possible complications, and also mentioned that if complications occur, they may need to convert to open surgery. How do you ensure that the patient agrees?
OptA: Take the bill of the procedure
OptB: Take verbal consent from the family
OptC: Write short notes with his consent
OptD: Write detailed notes including what the patient understood
why_right: Informed consent is valid only if the patient has understood the procedure, risks and alternatives, including the possible conversion to open surgery. Writing detailed notes including what the patient understood is the best evidence that real informed consent was obtained, alongside the signed form from the competent patient himself.
why_wrong_block:
A. Paying the bill shows a financial agreement, not informed consent to the operation. Payment has no role in proving understanding or agreement.
B. A competent adult gives his own consent; family consent is not valid and verbal consent is inadequate for a surgical procedure. Family consent applies only when the patient lacks capacity.
C. Short notes do not show that the risks, alternatives and conversion possibility were understood. Brief documentation is weak if the consent is later challenged.
key_concept:
Valid consent = capacity + information + understanding + voluntariness, documented.
  • Surgery: written consent by the competent patient
  • Document what was explained and what the patient understood
  • Include foreseeable changes (laparoscopic to open)
  • Family signs only if the patient lacks capacity
exam_pearl: The proof of consent is documented understanding, not a signature, a bill or a short note.

stem: A Researcher wants to do a research on a new screening test (I think). What the participant right?
OptB: You tell the positive cases about their diagnosis
OptC: Tell the negative about the diagnosis
why_right: A core right of every research participant is to withdraw at any time without penalty or loss of standard care, and this must be stated in the informed consent. It applies to every study, including one testing a new screening test.
why_wrong_block:
B. How results are returned to positive participants depends on the study protocol and what was agreed at consent, so it is not the universal participant right being asked for. It would be correct if the question asked how to handle a clinically important finding that the protocol commits to disclose.
C. Informing negative participants is likewise a protocol decision, not a fundamental right. It is not what defines participant protection in research ethics.
key_concept:
Research participant rights (informed consent elements):
  • Voluntary participation
  • Withdraw at any time without penalty
  • Know purpose, procedures, risks and benefits
  • Confidentiality of data
  • Ethics committee (IRB) approval before starting
exam_pearl: "Participant right" in research = free withdrawal at any time, without affecting their care.

stem: A nurse observes improper hygiene practices by a surgeon prior to surgery. What is the most appropriate action?
OptB: Politely inform the surgeon of the concern
OptC: Report to another physician to address the issue
OptD: Wait until after the surgery, then report to hospital authorities
highlight_terms_source: improper hygiene practices by a surgeon
why_right: The breach is happening prior to surgery, so the patient is at immediate risk of infection. Every team member has a duty to speak up, and the first step is to raise it directly and politely with the surgeon so it is corrected before the operation starts.
why_wrong_block:
A. Staying silent puts the patient at risk and fails the nurse's duty for patient safety. Silence is never correct when harm can still be prevented.
C. Going to another physician bypasses the person who can fix it right now and delays correction. Escalation to a senior is appropriate if the surgeon dismisses the concern.
D. Waiting until after the surgery lets the harm happen. Reporting to hospital authorities fits a repeated or ignored problem, after the immediate risk has been addressed.
key_concept:
Unsafe practice by a colleague, escalation ladder:
  • Immediate risk: speak to the person directly, now
  • Ignored: escalate to senior / head of department
  • Persistent or pattern: formal report to the institution
exam_pearl: If harm is still preventable, address it directly before the procedure; reporting later is the wrong timing.

stem: A woman undergoing a cesarean section has already signed consent for the procedure. During surgery, she develops severe, uncontrollable hemorrhage that does not respond to conservative measures. The surgeon decides that a hysterectomy is required to save her life. What is the most appropriate action?
OptA: Obtain consent from her husband before performing hysterectomy
OptB: Proceed with hysterectomy without consent because it is life-saving
OptC: Do only what she consented for and do not proceed with hysterectomy
highlight_terms_source: hysterectomy is required to save her life
why_right: She has uncontrollable hemorrhage unresponsive to conservative measures in the middle of the operation, so any delay to seek further consent would threaten her life. Under the doctrine of emergency necessity, a life-saving procedure can proceed without additional consent, ideally confirmed by a senior colleague and fully documented, with the patient informed as soon as possible.
why_wrong_block:
A. Her husband's consent is not what makes treatment of an adult woman lawful, and stopping to seek it delays a life-saving step. Surrogate consent applies only when a patient lacks capacity and the decision is not an immediate emergency.
C. Strictly limiting surgery to the original consent would let her die from a treatable cause. Sticking to the consented procedure is right when the extra step is not urgent and can wait until she can decide.
key_concept:
Emergency exception to consent:
  • Life or limb threatening, cannot wait
  • Patient unable to consent (anesthesia, unconscious)
  • No known prior refusal of that intervention
  • Confirm with a senior, document, inform patient afterwards
  • Contrast: a conscious competent patient who refuses must be respected
exam_pearl: Life-saving + cannot wait mid-operation = proceed and document; husband or father consent is never the answer for an adult woman.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Second recall in this block (next page): hysterectomy considered life-saving after consultation with a senior consultant; patient consented to CS only. A) Employ conservative measures until consent obtained, B) Proceed with the hysterectomy without additional consent (highlighted), C) Obtain consent from the father, D) Adhere strictly to initial consent.

stem: A doctor sends the cancer screening results to an elderly patient via his personal email, what is the problem with this?
OptA: Email may be accessed by unauthorized individuals
OptB: Patient may not understand the terms used in the email
OptC: Patient may have forgotten his password
why_right: The issue is confidentiality and data security: cancer screening results are sensitive health information, and a personal email account is not a secure channel. Others may access it, so results should go through secure, approved systems or be discussed directly with the patient.
why_wrong_block:
B. Unclear wording is a communication concern but not the core ethical problem with using personal email. It would be the issue if results were sent through a secure portal with unexplained jargon.
C. A forgotten password is a practical inconvenience, not an ethical or legal problem. It does not address the risk of exposure of his health data.
key_concept:
Sending health information electronically:
  • Use secure, institution-approved systems
  • Personal email or messaging apps: risk of unauthorized access
  • Sensitive or serious results: discuss directly with the patient
exam_pearl: Personal email for patient results = confidentiality breach risk; the elderly detail is a distractor.

stem: There is a question about a doctor who gave the wrong dose to a pt, and the nurse noticed. And the pt was discharged but came later with severe symptoms(or something like that) how to prevent that?
OptA: when any pt want to discharge his medications should be reviewed by a doctor
OptB: When prescribing drugs on the system an alert will show
OptC: The nurses should review the drugs after the doctor
why_right: The error was a wrong dose at prescribing that slipped through human checks. The most effective prevention is a system level fix at the point of prescribing: computerized order entry with dose alerts catches the error before it reaches the patient, rather than relying on people to notice.
why_wrong_block:
A. A doctor reviewing medications at discharge is another human check that can fail the same way, and it comes too late in the process. It helps reconciliation but is weaker than an automated safeguard at prescribing.
C. Nurse double checking adds a human layer, and in this case the error was noticed yet still reached the patient. Double checks are useful for high-alert drug administration but are weaker than system design.
key_concept:
Strength of error prevention measures:
  • Strongest: forcing functions, automation, computerized alerts
  • Intermediate: checklists, standardization, double checks
  • Weakest: education, training, warnings, policies
exam_pearl: "How to prevent" a prescribing error: pick the system fix (CPOE alert), not more human checking or training.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Another recall on the next page: HTN patient, doctor wrote wrong prescription, pharmacist noticed but thought doctor alert, patient developed severe BP drop; options: double check by nurse / patient review medication before leaving hospital / training to do best prescribing / (4) computerised physician order alert (highlighted; compiler notes the computer should alert when the doctor prescribes a large dose).

stem: As a doctor, you should respect patient autonomy. Which of the following is an example of respecting autonomy?
OptB: Protecting patient information
OptC: Treating patients equally and fairly
OptD: Obtaining patient informed consent
why_right: Autonomy is the patient's right to make decisions about their own body and care. Informed consent is its direct expression: the competent patient receives the information and decides for themselves, including the right to refuse.
why_wrong_block:
A. Covering patient bodies reflects respect for dignity and privacy, not decision making. It would answer a question about dignity or modesty.
B. Protecting patient information is confidentiality. It would be the answer to a question about privacy or confidentiality.
C. Treating patients equally and fairly is justice. It would answer a question about fair distribution of care or resources.
key_concept:
Four principles, classic examples:
  • Autonomy: informed consent, right to refuse
  • Beneficence: acting in the patient's best interest
  • Non-maleficence: avoiding harm
  • Justice: equal, fair treatment and resource allocation
  • Related duties: confidentiality, dignity and privacy
exam_pearl: Autonomy = the patient decides; consent and refusal are its examples.

stem: Patient DM HTN on medications admitted to the hospital to undergo a surgical procedure. After the operation he was transferred to the surgical ward but he was given IV morphine. Which of the following is the critical mistake in the scenario?
OptB: poor postoperative assessment
OptC: Pharmacy related
why_right: A patient with "DM HTN on medications" moved from admission to theatre to the surgical ward, and the new orders (IV morphine) were written without his home medication list being reconciled. Medication reconciliation means comparing the patient's current medicines with every new order at each transition of care (admission, transfer, discharge), so omissions, duplications and interactions (e.g. missed antihypertensives or diabetes therapy, sedative stacking with opioids) are caught. Its omission at the ward transfer is the critical system error in this scenario.
why_wrong_block:
B. Poor postoperative assessment is a clinical monitoring failure; the stem highlights a patient on chronic medications who changed care setting, which points to a reconciliation failure at the handover, not an assessment gap.
C. A pharmacy dispensing error would be the answer if the wrong drug or dose had been supplied by pharmacy; here the problem starts with the prescribing team not reconciling his existing medicines at transfer.
key_concept:
Medication reconciliation is required at every transition of care.
  • Transitions: admission, ward or unit transfer, postoperative transfer, discharge.
  • Steps: obtain the full home medication list, compare it with new orders, resolve discrepancies, document and communicate.
  • Errors prevented: omissions, duplications, dosing errors, drug interactions.
  • High-risk patients: multiple chronic diseases (DM, HTN), polypharmacy, opioid or sedative orders.
exam_pearl: Patient on chronic medications + change of care setting + new drug order = think medication reconciliation.

stem: Research for a group of cardiac patients: half will receive a new drug, and half will receive a placebo. Which of the following is correct for the patients?
OptB: Explaining and knowing the research instruments
OptC: Explaining the results of the procedure
OptD: Knowing if they receive the drug or the placebo
why_right: In a placebo-controlled drug trial, valid informed consent must tell participants that participation is voluntary and that they may withdraw at any time without penalty or any effect on their usual care. This right is a core, non-negotiable element of research consent (alongside purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, alternatives and confidentiality), so it is the true statement for these patients.
why_wrong_block:
B. Participants need a lay explanation of what will be done to them, but they are not required to know or understand the technical research instruments; this is not the key participant right.
C. The results of the study are not known in advance, so they cannot be explained at consent; participants are told the expected risks and benefits instead.
D. In a blinded placebo-controlled trial patients are told they may receive either drug or placebo but not which one; revealing allocation would break blinding (unblinding is only for safety reasons).
key_concept:
Research consent essentials (voluntary, informed, documented).
  • Purpose, procedures and duration of the study.
  • Foreseeable risks and possible benefits.
  • Alternatives to participation.
  • Confidentiality of data.
  • Voluntary participation and the right to withdraw at any time without penalty.
  • Placebo trials: patients know they may get placebo, not which arm they are in.
exam_pearl: "Knowing if they receive drug or placebo" sounds like transparency but breaks blinding; the protected right is withdrawal.

stem: A 30 yo female with a family hx of breast cancer in her mother when she was 45yo, she is requesting BRACA screening, did breast examination was normal. What to write on the consent?
OptA: discontinue the consoling as she has no symptoms
OptB: tell her the test will prevent future risk of ca
OptC: discuss emotional impact of positive test
OptD: tell her the test useless at her age
why_right: Pre-test genetic counselling for BRCA testing must cover the implications of a positive result: its psychological and emotional impact, the decisions it may lead to (intensified surveillance, risk-reducing surgery), and its implications for relatives. Discussing the emotional impact of a positive test is therefore an essential part of what she consents to, even though her breast examination is normal.
why_wrong_block:
A. Testing an asymptomatic woman is exactly the purpose of predictive genetic testing; having no symptoms is not a reason to stop counselling.
B. A BRCA test identifies inherited risk; it does not prevent cancer. Telling her it will prevent future risk is misleading and invalidates consent.
D. At 30 she is an adult able to consent, and a positive result would change her surveillance and risk-reducing options; the test is not useless at her age.
key_concept:
BRCA pre-test counselling (what goes in the consent).
  • What the test can and cannot tell her (risk, not diagnosis or prevention).
  • Possible results: positive, negative, variant of uncertain significance.
  • Emotional and psychological impact of a positive result.
  • Management options if positive: enhanced screening, risk-reducing surgery.
  • Implications for family members.
  • Confidentiality of the result.
exam_pearl: Any option that overstates what a genetic test does ("prevents cancer") is wrong; counselling must be honest about impact, not benefit.

stem: A pregnant woman with a history of complications in her previous pregnancies presents to your hospital with vaginal bleeding and is diagnosed with placenta previa. However, the hospital does not have adequate facilities to manage her condition. What is the most appropriate action?
OptA: Discharge her and provide a referral letter to a higher-level center.
OptB: Obtain her agreement for transfer to a higher-level center.
OptC: Tell her to go to a higher-level center on her own.
OptD: I don't recall
highlight_terms_source: hospital does not have adequate facilities
why_right: Placenta previa with vaginal bleeding can deteriorate suddenly into massive hemorrhage, and the hospital "does not have adequate facilities". The correct action is to stabilize her and arrange a proper facility-to-facility transfer, which requires her informed agreement after explaining why transfer is needed. Her consent respects autonomy, while the doctor still owns the safe, arranged transfer.
why_wrong_block:
A. Discharging an actively bleeding previa patient with only a referral letter abandons her to an unsupervised journey; she needs an arranged, escorted transfer.
C. Telling her to travel on her own is unsafe and amounts to patient abandonment; the referring doctor is responsible for organizing the transfer.
D. This is a recall placeholder, not a real management option.
key_concept:
Transfer of an unstable or high-risk patient: stabilize, consent, arrange, hand over.
  • Explain the need for transfer and obtain the patient's agreement.
  • Stabilize before transfer as far as possible (IV access, resuscitation).
  • Contact and secure acceptance from the receiving center.
  • Transfer with appropriate escort and documentation.
  • Never discharge an actively bleeding obstetric patient to self-transfer.
exam_pearl: "Discharge + referral letter" looks like referral but is abandonment in an active bleeder; pick the arranged transfer with consent.

stem: A pregnant woman came to the hospital with vaginal bleeding they discovered on MRI Placenta percreta. The hospital cannot tolerate this condition. What will you do as a physician?
OptB: Refer her upon patient's request
OptC: Discharge her with form of referral
OptD: Discharge her and tell her to go to tertiary hospital
why_right: Placenta percreta (placenta penetrating through the uterine wall) carries a high risk of catastrophic hemorrhage and needs a center with a multidisciplinary team and blood bank support. Since this hospital "cannot tolerate this condition", the physician must refer her and notify the receiving department directly (doctor-to-doctor handover, confirmed acceptance), so the transfer is safe and the team is ready on arrival.
why_wrong_block:
B. Referral is a medical decision driven by her condition, not something done only if the patient requests it; the doctor must initiate it (with her consent).
C. Discharging a bleeding patient with percreta with a referral form leaves her unmonitored during transfer and is unsafe.
D. Telling her to go to a tertiary hospital by herself is patient abandonment; the receiving team is not prepared and she may bleed en route.
key_concept:
Placenta accreta spectrum: keyword mapping and the referral rule.
  • Attaches to myometrium: accreta.
  • Invades myometrium: increta.
  • Penetrates through the uterine wall: percreta.
  • Major risk factor: previous uterine surgery, especially cesarean section.
  • Facility cannot manage: refer with direct notification of the receiving department, never discharge to self-transfer.
exam_pearl: A correct referral is active (call and hand over), not passive (letter or "go there yourself").
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1548).
