stem: A 10-year-old child with a severe neurological progressive condition is under the care of a pediatrician. The parents ask about the duration of a DNR order for their child. How should the DNR order be managed in this case?
OptB: DNR is reviewed annually
OptC: DNR is reviewed every 3 months
OptD: DNR is reviewed every 6 months
why_right: This recall's key is annual review: a DNR order is not permanent and must be revisited periodically and whenever the clinical picture changes. The clue is a "10-year-old" with a slowly "progressive" neurological condition followed by a pediatrician, i.e. a stable outpatient context, where yearly review is the keyed interval.
why_wrong_block:
A. A DNR is never valid for life: the patient's condition, prognosis and the family's wishes can change, so the order must be reviewed.
C. Very frequent review (every 3 months) fits an unstable or rapidly deteriorating patient or an inpatient setting, not a stable outpatient with a slowly progressive disease as here.
D. Nothing in the stem (no deterioration, no admission) calls for a shorter fixed interval; for a stable outpatient the keyed routine review is yearly, with earlier reassessment only if the condition changes.
key_concept:
DNR orders are time-limited and must be reviewed, not permanent.
  • Review periodically and with any significant change in condition
  • Stable outpatient chronic/progressive illness: this recall keys annual review
  • Each new admission or deterioration: reassess the order
  • Parents of a minor are part of the decision and its review
exam_pearl: "Valid for life" is always the trap: every DNR must be reviewed.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: B, the context goes with outpatient case.

stem: A scenario of a doctor who shared a medical report without consent. What is the justification?
OptA: A family member requested a report
OptB: It is a reportable disease
OptC: The patient is mentally incompetent
OptD: The hospital wants to share the case with the public media
highlight_terms_source: shared a medical report without consent
why_right: Disclosure without consent is justified only by a recognized exception to confidentiality, and the clearest one is a legal duty: a "reportable disease" (notifiable infection) must be reported to public health authorities to protect the community. The lead-in asks for the "justification", i.e. the legally accepted reason.
why_wrong_block:
A. A family member's request does not override confidentiality; a competent patient's information is shared with relatives only with the patient's consent.
C. Mental incompetence does not remove confidentiality; information goes to the legal guardian or surrogate decision maker for the purpose of care, not to anyone who asks.
D. Sharing a case with the media without consent is never justified; identifiable information requires the patient's explicit permission.
key_concept:
Breaching confidentiality without consent requires a legal or public safety justification.
  • Notifiable/reportable infectious diseases: report to public health
  • Court order or legal requirement
  • Serious risk of harm to others
  • Suspected child abuse
  • Family, employer, media: need patient consent
exam_pearl: A relative asking, even a close one, is never a justification by itself.

stem: A E-research group (E for electronic) wanted to see the effect of 2 different NSAIDS and their effects on Gastritis symptoms. Which of the following will make this research ethically lacking (not written like this, but the same idea)
OptB: Collecting the data will be hard
OptC: consent can't be fully insured
OptD: Privacy Could Be Invaded
why_right: The defining feature here is that the research is electronic ("E-research"): the main ethical weakness inherent to online data collection is the risk that participants' data and identity are exposed, so privacy and confidentiality could be invaded. The lead-in asks what makes this design ethically lacking, which points to the risk built into the electronic method.
why_wrong_block:
A. The right to withdraw at any time is a basic ethical requirement of every study; it is not something an electronic design takes away, so it is not the characteristic weakness of e-research.
B. Difficulty collecting data is a practical or feasibility problem, not an ethical one.
C. Valid informed consent can be obtained electronically (e-consent); the specific, recognized risk of online research is data privacy rather than impossibility of consent.
key_concept:
Electronic research: the core ethical risk is privacy and data confidentiality.
  • Protect identity: anonymize or de-identify data
  • Secure storage and transmission of data
  • Informed consent (can be electronic)
  • Right to withdraw always preserved
  • Feasibility issues are not ethical issues
exam_pearl: Separate ethical problems from practical ones: "hard to collect" is never the ethical answer.

stem: patient who signed DNR, after that he had surgery, during the surgery cardiac arrest (in OR) What should you do?
OptB: start resuscitation
why_right: This recall's key is to start resuscitation: an arrest "during the surgery" in the OR is usually caused by anesthesia or the procedure itself and is often rapidly reversible, so the DNR signed before surgery is treated as not covering this event. The clue is the setting ("in OR", intraoperative) rather than an arrest from progression of the underlying disease.
why_wrong_block: A. Respecting the DNR would be right for an arrest from the natural course of the patient's illness (e.g. on the ward), or if the DNR had been explicitly confirmed to continue in the operating room during the preoperative discussion.
key_concept:
Perioperative arrest in a DNR patient: the recall answer is resuscitate.
  • Intraoperative arrest is often iatrogenic and reversible
  • DNR status should be rediscussed before surgery (required reconsideration)
  • If DNR was explicitly kept for the OR: honour the agreed limits
  • Arrest from disease progression outside OR: respect DNR
exam_pearl: Location and cause flip it: OR arrest from anesthesia/surgery = resuscitate; ward arrest from the disease = respect DNR.

stem: You discussed the case with the physician for DNR of a patient and all agree on DNR, BUT the paperwork still not completed and the patient arrested on the OR table What to do?
OptB: Start resuscitation immediately
OptC: Respect patient wishes and don't resuscitate
why_right: Although everyone "agree[s] on DNR", the "paperwork still not completed", so no valid DNR order exists and the patient is full code. An arrest "on the OR table" demands immediate action, so resuscitation is started at once; the DNR documentation can be completed later.
why_wrong_block:
A. An ethics committee helps with persistent disagreement about goals of care, not with an arrest happening now; consulting it would delay life-saving CPR.
C. Withholding CPR would be right only with a valid, completed DNR order; a verbal agreement without documentation is not enough, and an intraoperative arrest is often reversible.
key_concept:
DNR must be documented to be valid.
  • Agreed but unsigned/undocumented DNR: resuscitate
  • Valid documented DNR: no CPR
  • Emergencies: act first, committees later
  • Ethics committee: unresolved conflicts, not acute arrest
exam_pearl: "Everyone agreed" is the bait; no completed paperwork means full code.

stem: patient with lung cancer and end respiratory failure, admitted with exacerbation he experienced a wish of DNR but his family believes that he will have a chance for recovery, but the "team uncertain about the true wishes of the patient it is written like this, what should the team prioritize first:
OptB: CPR immediately
OptC: Forgotten
OptD: documented patient preference regarding DNR
highlight_terms_source: family believes that he will have a chance for recovery
why_right: The patient himself expressed a wish for DNR, but the team is "uncertain about the true wishes". The first priority is to establish and rely on the patient's own documented preference, because a competent patient's autonomy outranks the family's hopes. The lead-in "prioritize first" points to clarifying the patient's wish before anything else.
why_wrong_block:
A. The family's wish does not override the patient's own expressed choice; family views matter only as surrogates when the patient's wishes cannot be known.
B. Immediate CPR ignores the patient's expressed DNR wish; it would be right only if he arrested with no valid DNR and no known preference.
C. This option was not recalled; whatever its text, the priority remains the patient's own documented preference.
key_concept:
End of life decisions: the patient's own wishes come first.
  • Competent patient: his decision stands
  • Uncertainty: check and document the patient's preference (advance directive, notes)
  • Family: surrogates only if the patient's wishes are unknown and he lacks capacity
  • Ongoing conflict: ethics committee
exam_pearl: Family insistence on "aggressive treatment" never outranks the patient's own stated wish.

stem: Elderly patient with advanced lung cancer presents acute exacerbation, he said to healthcare team please do not resuscitate or intubate in the future. His family insist to treat their father aggressively, thinking he will able to improve his condition. Healthcare team uncertain about patient wishes. Which of the following is first priority in this situation?
OptB: immediate resuscitation without consent
OptC: family members has privileges superior than patients wishes
OptD: documentation of patient wish regarding DNR
highlight_terms_source: please do not resuscitate or intubate
why_right: The patient clearly said "do not resuscitate or intubate", while the family wants aggressive care and the team is "uncertain". The "first priority" is to clarify and document the patient's own wish regarding DNR, because a competent adult's autonomy outranks the family's preference. Once documented, it guides all further decisions.
why_wrong_block:
A. An ethics board is a later step when conflict persists after the patient's wishes have been clarified and documented; it is not the first priority.
B. Resuscitation without consent contradicts the patient's explicit refusal of CPR and intubation; it is right only in an emergency where no valid refusal or DNR is known.
C. Families do not have rights superior to the patient's; they act as surrogates only when the patient lacks capacity and his wishes are unknown.
key_concept:
Conflict between patient and family on DNR: patient autonomy first.
  • Step 1: confirm and document the patient's wishes
  • Competent patient's refusal of CPR/intubation is binding
  • Family: informed and supported, but not decision makers over a competent patient
  • Persistent conflict: ethics committee
exam_pearl: "First priority" means clarify and document the patient's wish before involving committees.
compiler_note: ⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-1259 → B. Immediate resuscitation without consent. Confirm before the exam.

stem: Patient with advanced lung cancer and end stage respiratory failure, came with acute exacerbation of his condition, he has experienced the wish of DNR at the event of further decline, but his family insisted on aggressive therapy because they believe he will have recovery, the medical team uncertain about the patient's true wish What should the medical team prioritized at this situation?
OptA: Consult the ethics abroad for guidance
OptB: immediate resuscitation without consultation
OptC: family wishes over previous patient's decision
OptD: patient's documented preference regarding DNR
highlight_terms_source: uncertain about the patient's true wish
why_right: The patient "has experienced the wish of DNR" while the family insists on aggressive therapy and the team is unsure. The team should prioritize the patient's documented preference regarding DNR, because a competent patient's own decision outweighs the family's hope for recovery.
why_wrong_block:
A. An ethics committee is consulted when disagreement persists after the patient's documented wishes are established; it is not what is prioritized first.
B. Immediate resuscitation without consultation ignores the patient's stated DNR wish; it fits only an arrest with no known DNR or preference.
C. Family wishes never override a competent patient's prior decision; they guide care only when the patient's wishes are unknown and he cannot decide.
key_concept:
Patient's documented preference outranks family wishes.
  • Advance directive or documented DNR wish: honour it
  • Uncertainty: review records and clarify with the patient if possible
  • Family: surrogate only when the patient's wishes are unknown
  • Ethics committee: unresolved conflicts
exam_pearl: Hope for recovery from the family does not change a competent patient's DNR choice.

stem: A 19-month-old boy was brought to the Pediatric Clinic for ear infection. The nurse noticed the boy has not received any vaccination as recommended. The parents mentioned that they read that vaccinations are "bad to the boy brain". Which of the following is the most appropriate action?
OptA: Refer the parent for psychiatric evaluation
OptB: Accept since parent have full right to choose
OptC: Call social services to take over the custody
OptD: Correct the myth and explain the great benefit of vaccinations
why_right: The parents refuse vaccination because of misinformation ("bad to the boy brain"), so the most appropriate action is education: correct the myth with accurate information and explain the large benefit of vaccines. Vaccine hesitancy is managed by respectful counselling and catch-up vaccination, not by coercion or simple acceptance.
why_wrong_block:
A. Holding a mistaken belief from reading misinformation is not a psychiatric illness; psychiatric referral is unjustified and damages trust.
B. Accepting without counselling fails the duty to inform; parents' choice is respected only after they have received accurate information about benefits and risks.
C. Removing custody is reserved for serious abuse or neglect with risk of harm; vaccine hesitancy from misinformation is first addressed by education.
key_concept:
Vaccine hesitancy: educate first.
  • Explore the concern and correct misinformation
  • Explain benefits and real risks of vaccines
  • Offer catch-up vaccination for the unvaccinated child
  • Document counselling and any persistent refusal
  • Social services only for genuine neglect or abuse
exam_pearl: When a refusal is based on a myth, the answer is always to correct the myth before anything else.

stem: Child 7 years old had febrile seizure which was transferred by the EMD (emergency medical dispatch). The mother wants to inform the school regarding the child's condition. Which of the following is the role of EMD regarding the mother's concern ?
OptA: Advice taking consent before sharing the medical information
OptB: Advice the parents to share the medical information
OptC: Do not inform them
highlight_terms_source: mother wants to inform the school
why_right: The information belongs to the child, and the parents are the legal decision makers who hold it; the mother herself "wants to inform the school", so no one else's permission is needed. A school that knows about a febrile seizure can recognise a recurrence, give first aid and call for help, which is in the child's best interest. The EMD's role is therefore to support and advise the parents to share the relevant medical information.
why_wrong_block:
A. Consent is needed when a health professional wants to release information to a third party; here the parents themselves are the consent holders and are choosing to share, so asking them to obtain consent is circular.
C. Discouraging disclosure withholds safety relevant information from the people supervising the child daily and goes against the parents' autonomous, reasonable choice; it would only be right if the professional were being asked to disclose without parental agreement.
key_concept:
Confidential information is controlled by the patient, or by the parents/guardian for a child.
  • Parents may share their own child's medical information with the school freely.
  • A clinician disclosing to a third party needs the patient's/guardian's consent.
  • Sharing seizure history with a school helps staff recognise and manage a recurrence.
exam_pearl: Consent is required when the doctor discloses, not when the guardian chooses to share; the trap is picking "take consent first".

stem: Unconscious ectopic pregnancy Consent take :
OptB: don't do laparotomy
OptC: mange as a case of save living
why_right: An unconscious patient with an ectopic pregnancy is almost certainly a ruptured ectopic in haemorrhagic shock, which needs immediate laparotomy. She cannot consent and any delay risks death, so the emergency (implied consent) doctrine applies: treat as a life saving case and operate, documenting the reason. Consent is presumed because a reasonable person would want her life saved.
why_wrong_block:
A. Waiting for the family delays haemorrhage control in a life threatening emergency; relatives' consent is sought only when treatment can safely wait and the patient lacks capacity.
B. Withholding laparotomy leaves a ruptured ectopic bleeding; not operating would be appropriate only if she were stable and suitable for medical or expectant management, or had a valid prior refusal.
key_concept:
Emergency exception: life or limb threatening condition + patient unable to consent + no time = treat without consent.
  • Ruptured ectopic (shock, peritonism, shoulder tip pain, fluid in pouch of Douglas): surgery.
  • Stable, unruptured, small mass, low hCG, no cardiac activity: methotrexate is an option.
  • A competent patient's informed refusal must be respected even if life saving.
  • Document the emergency and inform the family afterwards.
exam_pearl: Conscious and competent refusing = respect the refusal; unconscious and bleeding = operate under implied consent.

stem: A 10-year-old child wants to participate in a clinical trial for asthma, but his parents refuse because they are afraid of possible adverse effects. What is the most appropriate next step?
OptB: Persuade the parents to let him join
OptC: Respect the parents wishes and remove him from the study
why_right: A 10 year old cannot give legal consent; enrolment of a child in research requires parental permission plus the child's assent, and both are needed. Because the parents refuse ("afraid of possible adverse effects"), the child must not be enrolled, and participation in research is always voluntary with freedom to withdraw. So the doctor respects the parents' decision and removes him from the study, which carries no penalty to his ongoing asthma care.
why_wrong_block:
A. Enrolling him against parental refusal violates informed consent and exposes a minor to research risk without valid permission; a child's wish (assent) alone is never sufficient.
B. Persuading or pressuring the parents is undue influence (coercion), which invalidates consent to research; investigators may give information but must not push for enrolment.
key_concept:
Paediatric research = parental permission AND child assent; either can block participation.
  • Child's assent sought from roughly school age, in age appropriate language.
  • Participation is voluntary; refusal or withdrawal must not affect standard care.
  • No coercion or undue inducement of parents or child.
  • Contrast: life saving treatment refused by parents may be overridden for the child's best interest; research participation is not.
exam_pearl: Parents' refusal to enrol their child in a trial must be respected; only refusal of life saving treatment can be overridden in the child's best interest.
compiler_note: Compiler note: A is unethical (Do No Harm). B is also unethical (Duress is immoral).

stem: A married couple underwent in vitro fertilization (IVF) and successfully created viable embryos. However, before the embryos could be implanted into the wife's uterus, the couple decided to get a divorce. What is the most appropriate ethical and legal action regarding the stored embryos?
OptA: Discard the embryos as they are no longer married
OptB: Keep the embryos stored until all legal matters end
OptC: Allow the wife to use the embryos since she has maternal rights
OptD: Donate the embryos to an infertile married couple
why_right: In the Saudi/Islamic framework, assisted reproduction is permitted only between a husband and wife during a valid, existing marriage, using their own gametes. Once the couple divorce, the marriage that made the embryos lawful has ended, so the stored embryos can no longer be implanted in the wife or given to anyone else and are discarded, which is what the regulations require on divorce or death of a spouse.
why_wrong_block:
B. Continued storage has no purpose because no future lawful use exists once the marriage is dissolved; prolonged storage pending litigation is a Western model, where embryo custody can be disputed in court.
C. Implanting the embryos in a now divorced woman would create a pregnancy outside marriage, which is not permitted; "maternal rights" do not override this.
D. Embryo donation introduces a third party into reproduction (like donor gametes or surrogacy), which is prohibited in Saudi Arabia.
key_concept:
Saudi ART rule: only husband's sperm + wife's egg + wife's uterus, within a valid marriage.
  • Divorce or death of either spouse: stored embryos are destroyed.
  • Donor sperm, donor eggs, donated embryos: not permitted.
  • Surrogacy: not permitted.
exam_pearl: In a Saudi exam, any option that brings a third party (donation, surrogate) or uses embryos after the marriage ends is wrong.

stem: A female patient undergoes BRCA genetic screening for breast cancer risk. Three days later, her sister arrives at the clinic asking to obtain the test results on her sister's behalf. What is the most appropriate action by the physician?
OptA: Refuse to disclose the results to protect patient confidentiality
OptB: Give the results to the sister as she shares a genetic risk
OptC: Refer the sister to the patient affairs department to sign a release form
OptD: Contact the patient immediately while the sister is in the clinic to get verbal consent
why_right: Test results belong to the patient who was tested, and they can be released to a third party only with the patient's own valid authorisation. A sister arriving on her behalf, even a close relative sharing genetic risk, has no right to the results, so the physician declines politely and protects confidentiality. The patient can then be informed herself and encouraged to share relevant genetic risk with her relatives.
why_wrong_block:
B. Shared genetic risk does not entitle a relative to another person's results; the correct route is to counsel the patient to inform her family, and the sister can seek her own genetic counselling and testing.
C. A release form signed by the sister is meaningless; only the patient can authorise disclosure, so this offers a false pathway around confidentiality.
D. Phoning the patient on the spot cannot reliably verify identity or free, informed consent, and genetic results should be disclosed to the patient first with proper counselling, not relayed through a relative.
key_concept:
Confidentiality: results go to the patient first; third parties need the patient's authorisation.
  • Relative requests results: refuse and advise them to ask the patient.
  • Genetic results: encourage the patient to inform at risk relatives.
  • The relative can get her own genetic counselling and testing.
  • Exceptions are narrow (court order, notifiable disease, serious risk to others).
exam_pearl: "Shares the genetic risk" sounds like a justification, but it is the trap: risk to relatives is handled by counselling the patient, not by breaching her confidentiality.

stem: 65 yo man Terminal lung cancer pt discussed his desire for DNR with his primary doctor, dnr order was NOT completed, then pt went for abdominal emergency surgery and during the surgery he had cardiac arrest, what to do?
OptA: respect pt previously mentioned desire for DNR
OptB: start Cardiac resus
OptC: obtain consent from family member
OptD: obtain consent from ethical committee
highlight_terms_source: during the surgery he had cardiac arrest
why_right: The patient only discussed a wish for DNR and the order was "NOT completed", so no valid DNR order exists. Without a documented DNR, the default for an in hospital cardiac arrest is full resuscitation, and this is especially true intraoperatively, where an arrest is often anaesthetic or surgical and reversible. The surgical team must start CPR immediately.
why_wrong_block:
A. A verbal wish relayed to another doctor is not an actionable DNR order; withholding CPR requires a properly completed, documented order, which would make this answer right.
C. Cardiac arrest gives no time to seek consent, and family members cannot create a DNR in the middle of an arrest; consent is implied for emergency resuscitation.
D. An ethics committee is for non urgent disputes about goals of care, not for a decision needed in seconds during an arrest.
key_concept:
No valid written DNR = full resuscitation.
  • DNR wishes must be converted into a signed, documented order to be honoured.
  • Before surgery, an existing DNR should be explicitly readdressed with the patient (suspend or maintain).
  • Intraoperative arrests are frequently reversible causes (drugs, bleeding, airway).
  • After the event, revisit goals of care and complete the DNR if still desired.
exam_pearl: "Discussed" or "wanted" DNR is not a DNR: if the order was not completed, resuscitate.

stem: A pregnant woman presented to the clinic. She is a high gravida and has done previous cesarean sections. She has metastatic cancer and her doctor advised for the termination of the pregnancy but her husband is refusing. What is the appropiate action?
OptA: You need both consent from her and husband
OptB: Only need her consent
OptC: Only need her consent and she should inform her husband
OptD: Obtain consent from a representative
why_right: The termination is advised because of a medical risk to the mother (metastatic cancer, high gravida, previous cesareans), so it is a therapeutic procedure for her own health. A competent adult patient consents for her own treatment, and the husband's refusal cannot block a medically necessary intervention. As with treatments that may cause sterility, consent is taken from the patient and she is asked to inform her husband, without needing his approval.
why_wrong_block:
A. Consent of both spouses is the usual rule for termination of pregnancy and shared reproductive decisions such as contraception, but here the procedure is needed for her own health, so her consent is sufficient and the husband's refusal does not block it.
B. Her consent is indeed the valid one, but this option omits the expected step of informing the husband, which preserves the marital relationship and is part of the recalled rule; C is the more complete answer.
D. A representative or surrogate consents only when the patient lacks capacity; this woman is competent and presented to clinic herself.
key_concept:
Competent adult = she consents for her own medically necessary treatment.
  • Spouse cannot sign in place of, or veto, a competent patient's consent.
  • Treatment needed for her health that affects fertility: her consent, she informs husband, his approval not required.
  • Shared reproductive decisions without maternal medical necessity (e.g. contraception): mutual consent expected.
  • Representative consent only if she lacks capacity.
exam_pearl: The fork is "medical necessity": for a risk to the mother, choose her consent plus informing the husband, not joint consent.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot: Answer: C (red pen tick), Usually consent is required from both parents for an abortion. But in this case there is a medical risk to the mother's wellbeing. Attached snippet on informed consent for treatment resulting in infertility/sterility: if treatment may lead to permanent sterility while there is a necessity for the medical intervention, informed consent is taken from the married patient and they are asked to inform their spouse without the need for their approval.

stem: Which of the following can a physician prescribe over the phone?
OptB: Methotrexate
OptC: Paracetamol
OptD: Nutrition feeding
why_right: This recall's key is nutrition/feeding: a diet or feeding order is a non-drug, low-risk order, so it is the one most acceptable as a verbal (phone) instruction. Drug prescriptions are expected to be written/entered by the prescriber, especially high-risk drugs.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antibiotics are drug prescriptions with allergy, dose and interaction risks; this source expects them to be documented by the prescriber rather than phoned in.
B. Methotrexate is a cytotoxic (chemotherapy) drug; verbal orders for chemotherapy are specifically prohibited in safety guidance, making it the clearest wrong choice.
C. Paracetamol is a low-risk drug that some recalls accept by phone (AS-1762), but here the key prefers the non-drug feeding order.
key_concept:
Phone/verbal order safety:
  • Avoid verbal orders except when urgent or prescriber cannot enter the order
  • Never for chemotherapy
  • Read back, document, prescriber co-signs
exam_pearl: Methotrexate is highlighted in one version of this recall, but it is the option that must never be ordered by phone; the compiler's typed key is nutrition feeding.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1764).

stem: Doctor prescribed warfarin for a women, in the next visit after one week he find that she is 10 weeks pregnant, what to do to prevent recurrence of this situation?
OptB: Tailor prescription to the individual
OptC: Knowing high-risk medications
OptD: Knowing generic names
why_right: Warfarin is a well known teratogen, so the error was not a lack of drug knowledge; the prescriber failed to check this woman's pregnancy status before prescribing. Preventing recurrence means tailoring each prescription to the individual patient: age, sex, reproductive status, comorbidities, allergies and co medications, including asking about pregnancy (and testing when in doubt) for any woman of childbearing age before giving a teratogen.
why_wrong_block:
A. Relying on memory is an error prone strategy that safe prescribing practice discourages; prescribers should use checks and references, not recall.
C. Knowing that warfarin is high risk was not the gap; the doctor still prescribed it because he did not know the patient was pregnant. This option would be right if the error came from unawareness of a drug's hazards.
D. Generic naming helps avoid duplication and brand confusion, but it does nothing to detect a contraindication specific to this patient.
key_concept:
Safe prescribing = right drug for this patient after checking her individual factors.
  • Women of reproductive age: ask LMP and pregnancy plans, test if unsure, before teratogens.
  • Warfarin in the first trimester causes warfarin embryopathy; heparins are used in pregnancy.
  • Also check renal/hepatic function, allergies, interactions.
exam_pearl: Ask what knowledge was actually missing: the drug's risk was known, the patient's pregnancy was not, so the fix is patient tailored prescribing.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot (item 168): The issue here is not that he did not know warfarin is high risk. He did not know the patient is pregnant! Therefore he did not tailor prescription SPECIFICALLY for this patient's history.

stem: DNR must be from same hospital / DNR from other hospital IS VALID for 24 hrs / Family should verify DNR patient / Any member of medical team can verify DNR
OptA: DNR must be from same hospital
OptB: DNR from other hospital IS VALID for 24 hrs
OptC: Family should verify DNR patient
OptD: Any member of medical team can verify DNR
why_right: Under the Saudi DNR guidance, when a patient is transferred from another national or international institution, a signed DNR order from the sending facility is valid for 24 hours. Within that window the receiving team must reassess the patient and, if appropriate, issue its own DNR order according to local policy.
why_wrong_block:
A. An outside DNR is not ignored on arrival; it is honoured temporarily for 24 hours to avoid an unwanted resuscitation before the receiving team reassesses.
C. In the Saudi framework the DNR is a medical decision made and documented by qualified physicians; the family is informed but does not verify or authorise it.
D. Not any team member can verify a DNR; it is a physician (consultant led) decision, while nurses and others follow the documented order.
key_concept:
Saudi DNR essentials:
  • DNR is a physician led medical decision, documented and signed.
  • Family are informed and counselled; their approval is not required.
  • DNR from another institution: valid 24 hours on transfer, then reassessed and reissued locally.
exam_pearl: Outside DNR is neither invalid nor indefinitely valid: remember the 24 hour bridge.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Options run together in recall; compiler states B) DNR from other hospital IS VALID for 24 hrs.

stem: A patient with a "Do Not Resuscitate" (DNR) order was transferred to another hospital. What is the most accurate statement?
OptA: DNR from another institution is valid for 6 months
OptB: DNR from another institution is valid for 24 hours
OptC: DNR from another institution is not valid
OptD: DNR from another institution is valid
why_right: Saudi DNR guidance states that on transferring or receiving a patient to or from another national or international facility, a signed DNR order from that facility is valid for 24 hours. This protects the patient's documented wishes during transition while the receiving physicians reassess and issue their own order if still appropriate.
why_wrong_block:
A. Six months is not the rule; a DNR from another institution is only a temporary bridge, and the receiving hospital must reassess within 24 hours.
C. Treating it as invalid could lead to resuscitating a patient against a properly made decision during the transfer period; it is honoured for 24 hours.
D. It is not valid indefinitely; after 24 hours it must be reviewed and replaced by the receiving facility's own DNR order.
key_concept:
Transferred DNR order (Saudi): valid 24 hours.
  • Receiving team reassesses within that window.
  • Continuing DNR requires a new local order by the responsible physicians.
  • Family informed, but the decision is medical.
exam_pearl: Watch the number: 24 hours, not 6 months, and not "invalid" or "valid" without a time limit.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot (item 108): Upon or during transferring or receiving a patient to/from other national or international health institutes, signed orders of DNR from other facilities are valid for 24 hours (Saudi DNR guidelines).
